items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

any of those suggestions will be well ca nvassed at the Business Committee when the

Power Prices—Electricity Market and Alternative Policies
1. GRANT ROBERTSON (D eputy Leader—Labour) to the Minister of Energy
and Resources : Has he been advised whether the Prime Minister agrees with the
Deputy Prime Minister that “a lot of us don’t li ke the power bills that we get” and if so,
has he been advised what action the Prime Minister proposes to take to reduce New
Zealanders’ power bills?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes, I have been
advised that the Prime Minister agrees with the Deputy Prime Minister’s actual
comment, as I do, which was: “A lot of us don’t like the power bills we get, but the one
thing that will be worse and more wasteful will be politicians running the electricity
system. And that will look cheap for a wh ile, and then you’ll find that the technology
hasn’t been upgraded, that the new generation that we need hasn’t actually turned up,
and then there’ll be a big spend by the G overnment to subsidise something and the
prices will go up.” I knew that the Deputy Prime Minister was a religious man; I did not
know he prophesied Labour-Green policy.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Have the Max Bradford reforms delivered cheaper electricity to
New Zealanders, as the National Party promis ed; if not, why is he so ideologically
blinkered that he is tied to a policy that will not lower power prices?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, given that I was about 12 at the time, it is hard to
recall. But I can say yes—yes, I think they did. Unfortunately, though, what happened
was a Labour Government where power prices went up by 72 percent, so it is hard to
disagree with what Rob Hosking said in the National Business Review  this morning,
which was that the Labour Party was full of power price gouges that took place between
9538 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Apr 2013

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why is the Minister so ideologically blinkered that he is tied to
an electricity system that means New Zealand consumers pay the second-highest
residential power prices in the OECD, despit e two-thirds of our power being generated
from cheap hydro, and where prices have risen at double the rate of inflation? Why is he
so tied to that system?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It is hard to take being called ideologically blinkered from
a party that wants to—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Down this end of the
House we could not hear half of that ques tion, because of the raucous noise from the
shameful person saying “What a shame.” and others. So perhaps we could hear it again.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am going to invite the me mber Grant Robertson to repeat
his question. This time there was so much noi se that I had trouble he aring the last part
of the question myself.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why is the Minister so ideologically blinkered that he is tied to
an electricity system that means New Zealand consumers pay the second-highest
residential power prices relative to industr y in the OECD, despit e two-thirds of our
power being generated from cheap hydro pow er, and where prices have risen at double
the rate of inflation since the Bradford reforms?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, it is hard to take criticism at being ideologically
blinkered from a party that wants to renationalise the electricity system. But be that as it
may, we have a very competitive system, wh ere actually in Christchurch right now, by
switching from the most expensive to the leas t expensive retailer, one can save nearly
$600 per annum. That is more than that party’s new policy would save.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does the Minister realise that there are 30 states in the United
States of America that use a similar si ngle-buyer model to the one proposed by the
Labour Party, and when will he be auditioning for Fox News, given his views?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: No, and as I have said, if the party opposite wants to
reintroduce some kind of Albanian energy policy, that is good for it, but this side of this
Parliament does not want that.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has he taken the Prime Minister to task for failing to deliver on
his promise to Grey Power in 2009 that his policies would “help constrain electricity
prices”, when power prices rose by at least fi ve times the rate of inflation over the last
year?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: How can I take the Prime Minister to task when he has, in
fact, met that quotation, given that under th at Government prices went up 72 percent
and under us they have been much more constrained, going up by only 20 percent.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Is the Minister aware of the M āori
Party’s policy to enact an annua l power rebate for low-income wh ānau, installation of
low-cost heating, and insulating 10,000 low-in come homes per year, including rental
properties, and does he agree th at the Government needs to look seriously at addressing
the quality of life for low-income families?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I was not aware of that policy. It sounds intriguing. Can I
say to the member that I think the best th ing we can do is to continue with our pro-
competitive drive that we started in 2010. The Electricity Authority is leading that, and
we are seeing real competition all thr oughout New Zealand, where nearly 700,000
people have switched from more expensive to less expensive retailers.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What does the Minister think of the M āori Party’s policy
of piloting insulation in homes in Ngati Porou and Ng āpuhi, two of the warmest areas
where Māori live, and how practical is that?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It sounds like good policy.
18 Apr 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 9539

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. It is very fortunate, or some
might say unfortunate, that the Minister does not have any responsibility for M āori
Party policy, so I think that question is out of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: He was talking about the M āori Party policy before to the
Minister in a question. The Minister answered it even though he had no responsibility,
and so he has allowed in my question on the same basis.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And on that basis too I think th e Minister is quite capable of
answering the question.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It sounds like very good policy and I think that the M āori
Party can share in the credit where this G overnment has now insulated nearly 230,000
homes, and will do by September of this year.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does the Minister realise that there is no functioning electricity
market in New Zealand under his Government’s  policy and that Labour ’s plan will see
incentives for new players to enter the generation and retail market and ensure that New
Zealanders will save at least 10 percent on their power bills? Why does he not want
New Zealanders to save 10 percent on their power bills?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: As I have said, the member opposite shows some sort of
Albanian economics understanding there. Th e fact of the matter is that under this
Government we have a very competitive syst em. There are 15 independent retailers at
work in this country competing against each other, and we have seen that with 700,000
different consumers changing from one to another.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Is the Minister aware that his own Government’s figures show that
average household power prices have soared in Tauranga at a rate 15 percent greater
than the rest of New Zealand, and what acti on does the Minister propose to take for the
people of Tauranga?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I think the people in Taura nga are exceptionally satisfied
with the political representation they get and the kind of quality el ectricity system they
get.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. How was that answering the
question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question was adequately addressed.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Has the Government considered New Zealand First’s proposal to
introduce a 10 percent discount subsidy from State-owned enterprise power companies
for SuperGold Card holders and pensioners who are struggling to meet winter power
bills; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: No. In fact, I met with Gr ey Power this week and we
talked through some of its co ncerns. I have explained, I thin k, the system that we have
and why it is becoming more competitive ev ery day. I have considered New Zealand
First policy, and, frankly, it is almost as loony as the Labour Party’s policy. What they
are effectively saying also is they want to see the power generators back in Government
hands, and I just think that is bad policy all round.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Further to the Minister’s previ ous answers, if the electricity
market is working so well under the Bradford model, which he favours, why have
electricity prices continued to rise and rise over the last decade?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, there are probably many reasons, and I do not
accept the basic proposition in the question. Bu t one reason would be the way the last
Government took so many dividends from the power companies, and that is why it is
now belatedly trying to apologise to the pe ople of New Zealand with, admittedly, some
“loony tunes” policy.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Are New Zealand residential c onsumers paying too much for
their power?
9540 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Apr 2013

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, every consumer thinks they are paying too much for
power, Mr Robertson. But the f act of the matter is that at the moment we have a
competitive system where there are options and where we have real security of
supply—something actually we could not have taken for granted unde r the last Labour
Government.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Although the Minister
went in the direction of that question, it was a straightforward question. It was not
whether New Zealanders thought they were paying too much for their power; it was
whether the Minister thought they were payi ng too much for their power. He said that
New Zealanders did think they were paying t oo much, but he did not  include himself in
that group.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Let us have the question again and the Minister can re-answer the
question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Are New Zealand residential c onsumers paying too much for
their power?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, with respect, the question is ill-conceived because it
is not a question of the price but whether it is competitive, and the system today is much
more competitive than it wa s under the Labour Govern ment. Since 2010, when we
implemented our reforms, we have seen it become more pro-competitive. It has still got
some way to go and I think, as  the Electricity Authority made clear yesterday, it is
getting better and better.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: On what basis does the Minist er claim that the market is
competitive when the same five companies control 93 percent of the generating and 95
percent of the retail market?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, of the many bases, how about this one? In Auckland
at the moment, if you switch from the most to  the least expensive retailer, you can save
$312; in Wellington, $212; in Christchurc h, $595; and in Balclutha, $419. That is
competition by anyone’s measure.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: So is the Minister telling us that he is comfortable with a market
in which five companies—the same five companies—control 93 percent of the
generating market and 95 percent of the retail market?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes, because what the member seems to ignore is that
there are, from there, six other players that , yes, are smaller, but are offering sharp
deals—like Ōpunake Hydro—and a number of othe r ones all around this country. We
have low barriers to entry a nd, frankly, I understand there is  something like four power
players at the moment that are looking at co ming in. So it is a ve ry sharp, competitive
system that, yes, could do better, but is getting better day by day.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, if this market is so sharp and so competitive, then how
come since National gained office, when demand has been flat, the price of electricity to
residential consumers has increased by 19 percent?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: There are a number of reasons. One is transmission costs
and the hundreds, perhaps small number of bill ions, of dollars that it is reasonable to
pass on. The fact of the matter is that under Labour-Greens policy we would not see
another dollar invested in transmission or generation by the private sector, because of
the economic lunacy of that—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister is
required to answer the question he was asked, not to give us his views of other political
parties’ policies. He is well into his answer  and half of it has now been devoted to
criticism of the questioner, and that is not satisfactory.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the Minister was addressing the question quite satisfactorily,
with some connotation. Has the Minister now finished his answer?
18 Apr 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 9541

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes.
Work Visas—Checkout Operators
2. Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Immigration
items.text: How many temporary work visas were issued for checkout operators in

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I am advised that
there were 49 occupational-specific temporar y work visas issued in the occupational
category of checkout operator in 2012. Of the number that can be identified by region,
more than 86 percent of them went to Otago—most likely to the Queenstown Lakes
district—and one was issued for the Auckland region.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : Were those visas subject to approvals in
principle; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I understand that the answer to that question is
no, and the reason is that the occupation of checkout operator is not on any of the skills
in demand lists that Immigration New Zealand would use to get agreements in principle
prior to somebody seeking employment.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: Given that 2,500 Kiwis queued for 7 hours to
apply for a mere 150 jobs at the Manukau C ountdown in January, how can the Minister
justify the issuing of temporary work visas for checkout operators, and can he explain
why Kiwis could not do these jobs?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, 2,500 is certainly a much larger number
than one, which is the number of checkout ope rator visas issued last  year in Auckland.
What that says to me is that Kiwis are lini ng up, they are looking for work, and they are
being successful in getting it.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : How can he justify 138,000 temporary
migrants’ work visas for jobs like chec kout operators when there were 162,000 Kiwis
on the unemployment benefit last year?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Very good. Well, the significant minority of
those visas were issued to international st udents who have work rights. As the member
may be aware, that industry is our second- largest service export ea rner behind tourism.
More than $2 billion a year is generated in this country from export education. And it is
the case that a good number are also working holiday scheme visa holders. That is a
reciprocal arrangement that we have with  a number of countries around the world. That
enables our Kiwis to see the world and to c ontribute to the richness of this nation, and I
think that is perfectly justified.
Cost of Living—Consumers Price Index and Power Prices
3. TODD McCLAY (National—Rotorua)  to the Minister of Finance : What have
been the recent trends in the cost of living for New Zealanders?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: I can report some very encouraging pr ogress, particularly with consumer
price inflation, food price in flation, and in electricity prices. That progress is
particularly stark when you compare the curre nt situation with th e first decade of the
century in the 9 years to 2008. Statistics New Zealand yesterday reported the CPI for
the year to March increased by just 0.9 percent. That was the fourth consecutive quarter
that annual consumer inflation has been 1 percent or less. This  is a considerable
improvement on consumer price inflation of more than 5 percent in late 2008, just
before this Government first took office. Comb ined with interest ra tes at 50-year lows,
this low inflation is delivering considerab le benefits to households and businesses
across New Zealand in terms of their standard of living.
9542 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Apr 2013

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What have been the main factor s contributing to annual inflation
remaining low at around 1 percent?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The consumer price index showed that in the past year the
price of telecommunication services fell 7.2 percent, audiovi sual and computing
equipment fell 12 percent, domestic airfares  fell 9.9 percent, and fresh milk was down
7.7 percent. Electricity prices did rise 5.2 per cent during the year. Most of that is due to
a one-off increase in the cost of transmission prices of getting the electricity to
households around New Zealand. In any event it is substantially less than the 8 percent
average—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Who believes the member? Who believes him?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —year-on-year increases in  the 9 years to 2008 when
people like Trevor Mallard we re in charge. In addition, the food price index fell 0.4
percent in the year to March. This was led by a 2.6 percent fall in grocery prices. Cheese
was down 9.1 percent and butter fell 22 percent. It is interesting to note that all of these
commodities are priced in a competitive ma rket, and the Government did not control
any price setting in any of them.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What reports has he seen on the price of electricity paid by hard-
working New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Electricity Authority yesterday released its review of
the electricity market in 2012. The report showed 18 percent of customers, around
32,000 people a month, voted with their feet by switching electricity providers in 2012,
presumably for lower prices. For the benefit of the Opposition, that is called
“competition”. Since November 2008 annual electricity price increases have halved
from the 8 percent year-on-year increases  suffered by hard-working New Zealanders
during the previous 9 years. This follows a number of pro-competitive reforms by this
Government, which apparently the Opposition is not aware of. We have reconfigured
State-owned enterprise assets to increase competition, created the Electricity Authority
and made it responsible for promoting competition, allowed line businesses to compete
in the retail space, and funded promotion of consumer switching through the What’s My
Number campaign.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Has the Minister seen any other proposals to tr y to lower electricity
prices?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, weirdly, yes, I have. Just before lunch today I
received one report, which I believe came from the “North Korean School of
Economics”. Apparently, the suggestion th ere was that nationalising the entire
electricity industry would somehow lead to lower power prices.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Surely it occurred to
you that a Minister cannot knowingly mislead the House. You and I know that he did
not receive anything from the “North Ko rean School of Economics”, and yet the
Minister got up and he said that he did. Perhaps you would like to bring him back to
order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not accept that point of or der. Would the Minister continue
with his answer.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If I could perhaps clarify my answer, I should clarify that I
received a report from the local branch of the “North Korean School of Economics”.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. You know full well
that there is no local branch, and—[ Interruption] No, no, no. The me mbers can treat it
with levity, but he is knowingly misleading the House. Please do your job.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister is entirely responsible for the content of his
answer. If the member thinks that there has been a misleading of the House, there is an
appropriate way to raise that matter, and the member knows that.
18 Apr 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 9543

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. In fact, I have two. The
first is a relatively simple one. You let the Government members barrack during the
right honourable member’s point of order. In fact, you almost looked like you were
going to do it yourself, from the way that you were laughing. Can I ask you to treat this
House—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is now ruining a perfectly fair point of order.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: —with impartiality.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And the second point?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The second point of
order is that you have alrea dy ruled that you do not  accept letters about matters of
privilege dealing with supplementary answer s. That was a supplementary answer. Are
you changing that rule?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No. With regard to the first que stion, the member is absolutely
right. Points of order should be heard in silence, and I certai nly do not encourage
barracking from either side dur ing a point of order. With re gard to the second point of
order, I make a decision on each alleged br each of privilege on a case by case basis.
Further supplementary questions—has the Minister finished his answer?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: He sat down.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, he was interrupted with a point of order.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: No, he sat down.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister was interrupted  with a point of order. He has
every right to complete his answer and will do so.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Just to accept the right honourable
member’s point, it certainly appeared to be the local branch of the “North Korean
School of Economics”, but I ac cept his assurance that pe rhaps it was not what it
appeared. Anyway, the suggestion was that na tionalising the entire electricity industry
would somehow lead to lower power prices. In  fact, as we have seen historically the
world over, it would simply lead to blackout s, higher prices, and considerably higher
costs on taxpayers. That is the “back to the 1970s Government” proposal by the Labour-
Greens coalition for running the electricity industry in this country.
Cost of Living—Impact of Price Increases and Access to Budgeting Services
4. Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere) to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: Does she agree with the CEO of Mangere Budgeting and Family
Support Services that “Increased private rental charges, higher power and energy prices,
higher costs for food and dairy, higher road user charges and incr eased petrol costs
etc…without putting up wages…means that  we are effectively making our people
poorer and ultimately it is costing the nation millions in welfare dollars”; if not, why
not?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have got huge
respect for the work that Darryl Evans and hi s team do on the front line, and I have no
doubt that the impact of the recession is ongoing and still having an effect for many. But
I also agree with this statement in the Otago Daily Times editorial from Tuesday: “New
Zealand has grasped the seriousness of a growing welfare class, and is mostly composed
about changes being made to encourage a hand-up, not a hand-out,”.
Su’a William Sio : Why does she believe that Work and Income grants to pay for
electricity and for gas triple d in a 2-year period, and wh at plans does her Government
have to address this significant increase?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We have seen hardship grants actually come down over
the last 2 years, and quite considerabl y—by about 33 percent. Wh at is interesting,
though, is that what we have is  that in 2009, 8 percent of all hardship applications were
9544 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Apr 2013
declined, and in October 2012 this proportion fluc tuated between 8 or 9 percent. So it is
not that more are being declined, it is that we are not taking as many. We do, as you can
see, actually accept more than we decline, certainly.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. My co lleague clearly asked
the Minister why she believed that electricity and gas gran ts had tripled in a 2-year
period. The Minister did not address that question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is absolutely a fair comment.  If the Minister would like, I can
have the question restated.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Sorry, Mr Speaker, I can be more specific if you like.
They obviously are paid out via hardship gran ts. What I have said is that overall they
have come down. What we are seeing, though, is  that people need assistance. That 2-
year period was through the recession and th rough the effects of that, and I am proud
that this Government has stood up and ma de sure that people can get the level of
assistance that they need.
Su’a William Sio : Is she aware that some families, according to budget advice
services, are forgoing food in order to be able  to pay for power bills  and are relying on
food parcels as a consequence; if so, what is her Government doing to address this?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: What I can say is that in 2008 under the previous
Government these budgeting se rvices and organisations were receiving just $4.3
million. Under this Government they are receiving a total of $13 million, so we are very
committed about giving them that level of  support, and recognising how they can
budget. They do have access to hardship grants, and we are providing them with
services and support wherever we can.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she assure the House that no budget advisers will be lost as a
result of the Community Response Fund comi ng to an end, given that budget advice is
now a prerequisite to accessing some Work and Income grants?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: What we can see is that this Government has more than
doubled the funding going to budgeti ng services over the last fe w years. This financial
year these budgeting services wi ll receive $13 million. That is  an increase on what they
received last year. We are ve ry cognisant of the fact that  they have pressure on them,
and, as a consequence, we are working closel y with them to see how we can work our
way through it.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she guarantee to this House that budget advice services will
continue to be funded at the same level th ey have been in past years, including the
Community Response Fund?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT

10. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Communications and Information Technology
items.text: How is the Government ensuring
telecommunications security legislation remains effective in a rapidly changing
telecommunications environment?
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): Yesterday I announced plans to modernise the Telecommunications
(Interception Capability) Act 2004. The proposed changes re late to obligations for
telecommunications companies and have tw o parts, one focused on modernising the
existing interception capability regime, and the second intr oducing a formal and
transparent framework for network security. The interception changes will continue to
require police or agencies to first obtain la wful authorisation to conduct surveillance, as
they currently must, and do not in any way ch ange the scope of what they are lawfully
able to intercept. New Zealanders who understand the importance of cyber security
know that it is essential that our regime keeps pace in a rapidly changing environment.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: Why are changes needed to inte rception capability and network
security?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: New Zealand’s telecommunications market has changed
significantly since the Act was passed in 2004. The changes proposed will make it
easier for telecommunications companies to understand and comply with their existing
interception capability obligations as these will be clearer and better targeted. Secondly,
although our network security regime has worked to date on the basis where companies
have worked cooperatively with the Govern ment, the increasing importance of cyber-
protection and the growing numbers of co mpanies involved mean that it is now
appropriate to move to a transparent and formalised regime.

11. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū) to the Minister of Housing : Does he

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Housing in Christchurch is a
challenge, but it is not a crisis. [ Interruption] Well, average rent s have gone up 10
percent, but are less than they are in either Auckland or We llington. Housing New
Zealand waiting lists for the highest nee d, A and B clients are currently 252—fewer
than there were prior to th e earthquakes and actually ha lf what there were under the
previous Labour Government. I also notice th at the numbers on the Christchurch City
Council’s waiting lists are fewe r than they were prior to the earthquakes. We have over

items.speaker: Phil Twyford

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH

Better Public Services Targets—Immunisation Health Report and Rates
12. Dr JACKIE BLUE (National)  to the Minister of Health : What reports has he
received on the Government’s better public service target for immunisation?
9554 Questions for Oral Answer 18 Apr 2013
Hon JO GOODHEW (Associat e Minister of Health) on behalf of the Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: Only 5 years ago New Zealand had one of  the lowest immunisation rates in the
developed world. Today I have seen reports th at 17 district health boards have achieved
the 85 percent immunisation target for 8-mont h-olds. This reflects  the hard work of
front-line immunisation teams. This means we  have again exceeded the national health

items.speaker: Dr Jackie Blue

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I move, That the
House note the Pacific Parliamentary Forum being held this week at Parliament and
that it acknowledge the needs and aspi rations of all Pacific peoples, and the
contribution New Zealand can make as an inte gral part of the Pacific region, to
enhance its relationship w ith all Pacific people . We are joined today in the House by a
number of special guests and delegates—
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9555

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the Minister, but we are joined today
by a number of very important guests, so  for those members who are leaving the
Chamber, I ask them to do so as quietly as possible.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: We are joined today in the House by a number of special
guests, the delegates attending the inaugural Pacific Parliamentary and Political Leaders
Forum. I would like to extend a very warm Aotearoa New Zealand welcome to each of
them. In particular, I welcome the Pacific Mi nisters here with us today. With your busy
schedules and various domestic pressures, it  is a great honour for New Zealand to host
you, as your cousins in the Pacific. I al so acknowledge the other members of the
delegation. You represent the leaders and decision makers of tomorrow. It is a privilege
to have you here, and I look forward, together w ith all members of our Parliament, to
meeting many of you over the coming days.
I would like to acknowledge the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee that
in 2010 unanimously recommended to the Hous e this interaction between our Pacific
parliaments. I would like to congratulate my colleague John  Hayes MP, as chair of the
committee, on the work he has led to bring th e original recommendation to fruition. To
all those who have helped: ng ā mihi nui. I would also like to take this opportunity to
acknowledge my colleagues across the House who are of Pacific descent, and whose
presence here adds richness not only to their respective parties and communities but to
our Parliament as a whole.
The Pacific is a key priority for the Na tional-led Government, as it has been for
successive New Zealand Governments over many decades. We are a Pacific nation.
First and foremost, we are united by the gr eat ocean Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, which joins
us, and that is central to our understanding  of our history, cu lture, and world view.
Culturally, New Zealand owes much to othe r Pacific nations. Around 7 percent of New
Zealanders are of Pasifika  origin. At the time of the 2006 census New Zealand’s
population included some 58,000 Cook Isla nders, 22,500 Niueans, 6,900 Tokelauans,
131,000 Samoans, 50,000 Tongans, 9,900 Fijians, and 8,900 other Pacific peoples. In
the case of the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, with whom we share particular
constitutional relationships , the New Zealand - based p opulations are significantly
higher than those based in th eir home countries. All of thes e Pacific peoples add to the
social and economic fabric of this great country, and we are richer for their presence.
The many ties that link New Zealand across the Pacific make the fate of Pacific
Island countries a matter of personal interest to many New Zealanders, not least because
of the significant contributions that Pasi fika people make, whether Pacific or New
Zealand - born, to the strength of our economy, the dynamism of our communities, and
the richness of our culture. Pacific Isla nd nations have gifted us and pushed out
boundaries in art, literature, dance, music,  film, fashion; with experts in health,
education, finance, and the economy; leaders and politicians at co mmunity, local, and
central government; and, of cour se, sport in every arena. New Zealand’s universities,
hospitals, art galleries , Government agencies, schools, bu sinesses, and Parliament have
much to be thankful for in terms of the contributions made by our Pacific communities,
all wrapped and delivered through language , identity, and culture, and long may it
continue.
Economically, our exports to Pacific Island count ries total nearly  $1 billion. The
region, considered in its entirety, repres ents New Zealand’s se venth-largest export
market and twentieth-largest trading bloc. Trade with the region has grown more than
30 percent in the last 10 years, and our exports have grown by 50 percent. New Zealand
industry is working hard to provide the goods  and services the economies of the Pacific
need. At the same time, demand in New Z ealand for Pacific goods, and particularly
Pacific agricultural products, is on the rise  too. Imports in this sector have nearly
9556 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
doubled since 2000 and are expand ing to include a greater ra nge of quality products.
Moving forward, Pacific engagement in PACER-Plus negotiations will strengthen
economic relationships and enhance regional capacity for trade.
This Government has an absolute focus on, and commitment t o, supporting Pacific
countries and New Zealand’s Pacific comm unities in achieving their developmental
aspirations. Not only are we committed to work ing with our Pacific partners to achieve
success, our results tell us we  are making a real and meani ngful difference in people’s
lives. The most readily visible demonstrati on of this Government’s commitment to the
Pacific is that we spend more than half  of our annual overseas  development budget,
more than $250 million, in the Pacific. Ever y day, staff from the Ministry of Foreign
Affairs and Trade are work ing alongside their Pacific counterparts to deliver
programmes that will assist Pacific countries to improve  their economic performance
and support them to achieve sustainable economic growth.
Key recent successes that serve as examples  of the progress being achieved by our
Government include renewable energy. The Pa cific Energy Summit, held in Auckland
last month, underlined the commitment New Zealand has made to working with the
Pacific to assist in channell ing international funding to areas of greatest need. Over 600
delegates attended the summit, including eight Prime Ministers, three Presidents, and 75
chief executive officers. A key outcome of the summit included securing donor
commitments of $635 million to advance renewa ble energy projects across the Pacific.
In addition to working with developed part ners to secure and channel development
assistance, New Zealand announced $65 million of  funding to assist Pacific Islands to
realise their renewable ener gy and energy-efficiency plan s. Support was announced for
the Cook Islands, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu.
In fisheries, the Pacific tuna stock repres ents the Pacific region’s greatest shared
resource. It continues to be a main source of income in the Pacific, contributing US$260
million to combined gross domestic product and providing over 13,000 jobs to Pacific
Island people. During the 2012 Pacific Islands  Forum, Prime Minister Key announced
New Zealand would invest additional fundi ng into fisheries s upport programmes,
bringing our total commitment over the ne xt 4 years to $50 million. Our support is
aimed at upgrading the Pacific’s fisherie s training institutions, fostering seafood
business enterprise development, helping pe ople in the industry gain formal, globally
recognised qualifications, and upskilling fisher ies officials in areas like international
commerce and investment appraisal.
The Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme helps to address seasonal labour and
skill shortages in the horticulture and viticulture industries that cannot be filled from the
available New Zealand labour pool. For the last 3 years between 6,000 and 7,000
Recognised Seasonal Employer workers have arrived in New Zealand annually.
Because I am running out of time because ther e is so much to say, I want to quickly
flip to the end of my prepared speech and talk about how important it is that this
inaugural parliamentary and political leader s meeting is occurring. I want to touch
briefly on the issue of democracy, a key them e of the upcoming Pacific Forum. One of
the values we share with our Pacific neighbours is a commitment to parliamentary
democracy. In the Pacific context, different States have devised their own ways to shape
and scale the democratic model and style to suit their situation. New Zealand is proud to
stand by our Pacific partners and actively  support the functioning of democracy in the
Pacific. New Zealand is and will rema in a committed supporter of the Pacific’s
democratic traditions, and I have no doubt that  we will remain ready to support Pacific
countries as and when our assistance is requested.
Finally, it would be unconscionable not to raise the issue of the low representation of
Pacific women in their Parliaments. Just as ours in New Zealand has been the better for
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9557
the strong participation by women member s of Parliament, so too will be the
parliaments of the Pacific Island nations. We should all work towards that goal.
I would again like to thank our distingu ished guests for their attendance at the
inaugural Pacific Parliamentary and Political Leaders Forum. We want you to know that
we are committed to working with you as our Pacific partners to improve the lives of
people throughout the Pacific. We are also committed to working to improve the lives
of members of our Pacific community in Ne w Zealand. The Government is mindful of
New Zealand’s place as a Pacific country. We  are honouring that by working to build a
brighter Pacific future in which all Pacific people can share. Tēnā koutou katoa.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Talofa lava, malo e lelei, kia
orana, taloha ni, bula vinaka. I could go on and on, because there are 22 different
greetings that I could give today. I just want  to say warm Pacific greetings to you all.
Tēnā koutou katoa. I hope you are enjoying the Wellington weather. If you think this is
bad, you should see it on a really bad day. Th is is my Wellington compatriot Grant
Robertson here beside me. It is wonderful to have you here with us today. As I say,
there are 70 different delegates from 22 different nations.
Aotearoa New Zealand is a Pacific nation. It  is geographically where we live. More
than 20 percent of our population is Polynesian—either Māori or Pacific migrants. They
are descendants particularly from Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau,
with which New Zealand has very close relationships. Auckland is the largest
Polynesian city in the world. The gateway to Auckland is guarded by Su’a William Sio,
the member for M āngere, who says that he will be staying there for a long time. The
gateway to Wellington is guarded by Kris Faafoi. If you are going through Mana, that is
his patch. So two of our Pacific MPs guard the entrance to two of our biggest cities.
Pacific nations are—

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What about us?

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: And over there—Sam, you are so rt of in the middle. You pass
through Sam’s electorate when you are going somewhere else.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member must
use the member’s full name.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: The Pacific nations are our ne ighbours in the Pacific region,
but they are also our neighbours in our street s—and in my street, in particular—so it is
quite a unique relationship that we have. Pa sifika people are ove rrepresented in our
teams, particularly our rugby teams and our  rugby league teams. One of the great
problems about the emigration to Australia is th at we are losing some of our best talent,
which we would rather have here, and giving it to our Australian opponents.
Although much in our culture and heritage has come from our European ancestry and
we are an increasingly multicultural country, P acific influences have shaped the unique
character of us as New Zealanders. We are part of the Pacific, and as a small country we
look as a priority to making a contribution in the neighbourhood in which we live. We
are committed to working with our neighbours to realise the vision set out by the Pacific
Islands Forum leaders that our region shoul d be one of peace, harmony, security, and
economic prosperity. It makes sense for our el ected representatives and leaders to come
together to discuss the issues and challenge s that confront our region, and to work
together to enhance the lives of all our pe oples. One outcome will be that we get to
know each other better and develop habits of cooperating and collaborating on a much
more regular basis. The Pacific Islands Forum, as you know, is now in its 40 th year, and
it provides an opportunity for Prime Ministers,  leaders, and Foreign Ministers to get
together for talks.
This forum today is the initiative of our Pa rliament, and I recognise the role that has
been played by the Foreign Affairs, Defen ce and Trade Committee, by its chairperson,
9558 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
John Hayes, and by the other members of that  team to bring together and enhance the
cooperation between parliaments and between parliamentarians. Once again I say that it
is a great pleasure and an honour to welcome you here.
Democracy is a common feature in our re gion. We know that democracy is a fragile
thing, and one of the goals of this conference is to discuss how we can make democracy
and the effectiveness and responsiveness of our parliaments that much better.
Democracy needs a free media. It needs an  independent and strong judiciary. It needs
institutions that guarant ee and protect human rights.  It requires openness and
transparency. All of those things help to protect the rights of people. It also needs
properly functioning political parties to help bring order, efficiency, and predictability
to the way our political system operates.
I hope you were not put off too much by ou r question time. That  is what we call
robustness of debate and holding the Governme nt to account. It is going to be so much
better when we are on that si de of the House and we have  to answer the questions,
rather than on this side, where we have to ask them.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: It won’t be long.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: It will not be long. We are counting down the days. I have got
a calendar on my wall, and I am just ticking them off.
Good governance, in turn, helps us to achie ve economic development and the social
services that people need in order to lead secure and fulfilling lives.
The global financial crisis, as we know, revealed just how fragile the economies of
many countries in our region actually are. E xport levels and growth have fallen. Some
countries have had to face real debt prob lems. We know others have vast natural
resources, and yet others are less well-e ndowed. We need to focus on how we develop
the strengths of our regions—through fisher ies, through our tropical agriculture, and
through tourism—and reduce the dependence on imported fossil fuels.
We also need to help build infrastructure and develop our human resources. We need
to create decent transport and communication links. I, for one, would like to see better
links around the Pacific so our relatives can get to family weddings and to funerals. I am
actually reminded, as I say that, of The La ughing Samoans, whom many of you might
know, who do travel around the Pacific every year. They make money out of making
people laugh, which I have to say must be  a great occupation. Some people say that
politicians are a bit like that, as well.
Economic development must be sustainable. It must benefit all of the people in a
country, not just its elite. Most particular ly, we know that our e nvironment is fragile,
and that our economic development must be  environmentally sound. The Pacific is a
beautiful region, but the reality  is that the region is not as picture postcard - like
underneath as it might seem. We have some  real challenges, ce rtainly socially and
economically. We are well off-track with th e UN Millennium Development Goals, for
example. So there are big challenges, and we need to work together to try to resolve
them.
It is appropriate, therefore, that half of our development assistance is directed at the
Pacific, something that actually was not the case for quite a long time until the Labour
Government, and I am pleased that the National Government has continued the trend—I
mean that sincerely—to focus assistance in that direction. But ach ieving better results
for the Pacific also requires old and new donor nations to work together and support
each other. It is important to work with not just countries like Australia, Japan, and the
EU but also China, which is on-track to become the world’s largest economy. We have
to work cooperatively with all of those partners.
Finally, there are other areas where New Zeal and can continue to play a key role and
support. In particular, what we call our Project Protector cr eated significant new
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9559
resources in our navy. We have a small but  perfectly formed Defence Force, which
actually is getting smaller by the day under this Government. Nevertheless, we have as
part of those resources a multi-role vessel,  and inshore and offshore patrol vessels,
which can help with search and rescue, with  fisheries protection, a nd with dealing with
the impacts of natural disasters such as cyclones and tsunamis. Those assets were
purchased with the primary focus being to work more positively in the Pacific.
This conference is not about, obviously, tellin g Pacific countries what they want or
what they should do. It is about working together as the neighbours that we are, learning
together, and collaborating to  find solutions to the problems and challenges that we
face. I hope that the conferen ce is not just a one-off event—once again, I congratulate
the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee for its foresight—but rather is a first
step in a parliamentary dialogue and decision-making process that can be expanded, and
that can be, therefore, a foundation for fu rther and ongoing parliamentary cooperation.
Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koutou
katoa ng ā rangatira o Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa. T ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou
katoa. Aotearoa New Zealand is still in the early stages of its identity as a 21 st century
Pacific nation. For M āori, of course—ng ā iwi M āori—we are ng ā uri o Te Moana-nui-
a-Kiwa; we always have been, and we always will be. We are not Europe; we are the
Pacific. But in more recent times since colonisation that identity, that sense of place and
belonging, has been a bit of a struggle, and that identity struggle has meant that New
Zealand’s actions in the Paci fic have been at times honourable and at times deeply
wrong.
Our honourable moments have included joining in the fight to stop French testing of
nuclear bombs in Pacific waters, and a rapi d and compassionate response to the natural
disasters that afflict Pacific nations. Ou r questionable actions have included, for
example, New Zealand’s neglect on climate ch ange, and to that e nd the Greens believe
that New Zealand should increase our commitme nt to climate financing for the Pacific,
and my colleague Kennedy Graham—responsible  for global affairs—will address that
issue later in the debate. Other questionable actions by New Zealand over the years
include the dawn raids; the Citizenship (W estern Samoa) Act, which took away from
Samoan citizens here their ri ght to that citizenship; a nd, of course, the continuing
poverty that is suffered by Pasifika children here in Aotearoa.
So as we welcome representatives from our tu ākana sovereign Pacific nations, we
should reflect on how we as a nation treat their citizens in our own country. My priority,
of course, is the well-being of New Zealand’s children, from all cultures. It is with some
shame that we reflect on the situation of Pasifika children living here. As a Pacific
country, we have a blood obligation to our Pacific wh ānau, and yet we have failed in
that duty—40 percent of Pasifika children live in poverty in Aotearoa New Zealand. A
similar percentage of young Pasifika are wi thout work in Aotearoa New Zealand. We
continue to harass and deport the parents of Pasifika chil dren, who are themselves New
Zealand citizens but their pare nts are not. We fail to ensure that the economy works to
provide decent jobs at decent pay so that, for example, Jaine Ikurere, a Pasifika woman
who cleans John Key’s office here at Parlia ment, does not earn just above the minimum
wage but has a living wage, which she can use to provide properly for her children and
her grandchildren. This is what a decent c ountry does, what a decent community does,
for its whānau. We are whanaunga to the Pacific iwi whom we welcome today, and we
must express that whanaungatanga in all policy and decisions that we make as a
Parliament.
The Greens have long advocated for human rights issues in the Pacific, and good
governance as well, starting, of  course, with Fiji. We are also particularly concerned
9560 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
with human rights abuses that result from the colonisation that has occurred in the
Pacific and continues to occu r in the Pacific. My colle ague Catherine Delahunty has
been very involved in the human rights i ssues concerning West Papua, and recently,
along with others, supported the New Zeal and tour of Benny Wenda, a West Papuan
freedom fighter. Unfortunately , Benny Wenda was refused the courtesy of holding a
meeting here in Parliament to talk to members of this Parliament about the human rights
issues facing his people. These are the expe riences that we as parliamentarians in
Aotearoa need to understand. The first step to that understanding is being prepared to
listen to Pacific peoples tell their stories to us face to face, kanohi ki te kanohi.
The Green Party urges our Government and all other Pacific Governments to provide
leadership on the issue of West Papuan i ndependence and human rights. This can be
done by offering to mediate peace between Indonesia and West Papua leaders, and
supporting West Papua becoming a member of  the Melanesian Spearhead Group and of
the Pacific Islands Forum. The State-sanc tioned violence and human rights abuses
against West Papuans require s all the Pacific neighbours to  support an end to the ban
against independent journalist s reporting on West Papua and, of course, to have the
courage of our convictions on the sad and sorry s ecret of the Pacific region. We are our
brothers’ and our sisters’ keepers, after all.
This is why the Greens have also been such strong advo cates of gender balance and
women’s representation in Pa cific parliaments, includi ng our own. There is no better
advocate for women than women themselves, who have lived the same lives as their
constituents and understand both the needs and the strengths of women. To this end, we
have worked with others to support Pa cific women standing fo r election in many
different Pacific countries. The gender balance in Pacific Island parliaments is certainly
improving, but there is still a long way to go. Here, MMP has significantly increased the
representation of M āori women as well as Pasifika women and other women of
ethnicity. Structural changes to electoral systems are neces sary to combat entrenched
gender inequity.
Overall, the numbers of Pacific women MPs across the region are growing, and there
are some strong strategies for continuing this trend. One option is to implement
electoral quotas, so that members are elected by pr oportional representation. France,
apparently, implemented a statutory require ment for parties to alternate candidates
based on gender, and these zipper lists have contributed to a high number of women in
the French Polynesian and New Caledonian  parliaments. Another option could be
reserve seats, and I understand Bougainville cu rrently has those. Reserve seats can help
change attitudes, increase acc eptance of women in public l eadership roles, and ensure
that their voices are heard. There is currently a bill before the Samoan Parliament, I
understand, that would guarantee th at at least 10 percent of seats would be held by
women. I will be very keen to see how this progresses, and whether we can offer any
assistance to women in Samoa around this issue. Each nation will, of course, develop
different systems to assist with gender ba lance in its Parliament, according to the way
that it operates. We certainly look forwar d to working more cl osely with Pasifika
women’s organisations to help progress gender equity in Parliaments.
Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, the ocean, sustains th e Pacific. The Pacifi c’s fisheries have
been described as being as important to th e region as oil is to the Middle East. New
Zealand has a supporting role in the issues  surrounding Pacific fisheries. There is
significant worth in strengthening the manage ment of Pacific fisheries in order to
safeguard their value and maxi mise the economic and social benefits of fisheries to
Pacific Island countries. One issue of partic ular relevance here is the conservation of
tuna stocks and protection ag ainst overfishing—although ther e are the eels, the “tuna”,
which also deserve to be protected and whic h have a life cycle that takes them from
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9561
Aotearoa waters out to the Tonga Trenc h—so tuna and “tuna”.  Sorry, that was a
distraction—my apologies.
One issue of particular relevance here is  the conservation of tuna stocks and the
protection against overfishing. Tuna stocks in other parts of the world have been
severely depleted by overfishing, and this serves as a cautiona ry tale, of course, for the
Pacific, as we all know. The key Pacifi c tuna stocks are now approaching their
sustainable limits. We must take action to maintain the productivity  of this valuable
resource. The Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Convention is the regional fisheries
management organisation charged with the conservation and management of this highly
migratory fish stock. Close cooperation between all the Paci fic nations, including
Aotearoa New Zealand, is necessary, so that we speak with a united and clear voice
about the need to promote and conserve this resource.
Finally, there are many issues for the Paci fic Parliamentary and Political Leaders
Forum to discuss, not least of which is how  we in Aotearoa New Zealand intend to
address our own attitude to the tu ākana whom we welcome today. Aotearoa New
Zealand is teina to the Pacific, to those in the Pacific who have been sovereign in their
lands for centuries longer than the m odern New Zealand has been around.
Remembering this, we can dem onstrate our respect to our tu ākana, to our elders; re-
establish our wh ānau connection with them; and meet our obligations proudly as uri o
Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa. Tēnā koutou katoa.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Kia ora. T ēnā koutou katoa,
and warm Pacific greetings. It is a privileg e to welcome our esteemed guests to this
significant event and meeting. It is hoped that by this we will strengthen New Zealand’s
relationship with the Pacific region and th e countries and peopl es within it. The
populated Pacific region is extraordinarily la rge, encompassing about one quarter of the
world’s surface. The populations may be low, but they are high in resources. It is, after
all, our backyard and our neighbourhood.
Your presence here today is a timely reminder that one value we share as a region is
a commitment to democratic values. It might be painful and difficult, but we do believe
that we should elect the people who repres ent us. The record is not perfect and the
failures stand out, but today provides us all with a chance to look past the failings,
discuss what went wrong, and plan for the future. On behalf of New Zealand First—that
is the people’s party, by the way, in th is country—and my colleague Asenati Lole-
Taylor, welcome to you all and thank you for coming.
This region is one of rich culture, lands capes, and natural wealth. It is a region
known for its striking artworks and its str ong, proud people. It is a region of great
potential. These resources held here hold the promise to generate adequate sources of
income for the Pacific if they are handled  right, whether that be in relation to
agriculture, horticulture, tourism, or critic al areas such as fishing and the fishing
resource. Pacific countries and people in the Pacific realise and recognise this fact. In
acting to secure their people a prosperous future in the 21 st century, this region is fast
becoming a platform for other small island States around the world to learn from.
We play an important role in the Pacific region. We have of late, I am very pleased to
say, over the last 10 years, realised that we should be spending far more of our foreign
aid in our area where we know the people than in far-flung ar eas where we have got no
idea where it is going.  I think we are probably all united on that. We have about
300,000 Pacific people in this country, and New Zealand needs to play its part to ensure
that Pacific people receive the means to be self-reliant and self-sufficient. Aid should be
seen as an investment. We recognise that  our Pacific neighbours are proud people, and
we recognise that aid is not a handout; it is a hand up. And above all, my party for one
9562 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
recognises that when dealing with the Pacific you are dealing with people who are in
every way your equal, and many have been here for millennia.
It is in New Zealand’s interest to see a flourishing Pacific region. We understand that
poverty and social ills lead towards political and social unrest. We want a stable region
that is prosperous, with strong trade links and a strong diffusion of ideas. If someone
suggests to you that the aid thi ng is not quite right, remember the fact is that for every
$10 that we export, $1 is coming back. The ratio, with regard to your people, is 10:1,
and we have no trading relationship that has th at percentage of benefit for this country
as it is with the Pacific people. If we had that ratio around the rest of the world, we
would be enormously rich, and we need to address that when we are explaining why aid
is important in this part of the world.
In a geopolitical sense the Pacific region is fast becoming an area of competing
influence, and it is a sense of disquiet that one  has. This is due in part to the region’s
proximity to Asia, natural re sources, and a number of votes  in the United Nations. We
all know how seductive it is to be taken down the main drag in China, with motorbikes
all in front and motorbikes all behind, and treated like you are a god. But that reminds
me of the old saying that new Caesars used to  be told when they were appointed in the
old Roman days. There was always a person deputed to run by their side and every now
and again say: “Remember, you’re only a man—remember, you’re only a man.” That
seductive experience in the Pacific with Asia  has to be carefully, carefully handled. Do
not worry. I have got colleagues like that myself who get totally carried away when they
go overseas and forget that their roots lie in their own country. Can I just say—

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: What about a mirror?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, no, no, no. I am a Pacifi c person. Our roots here
go back a thousand years—just in case any of you were not certain of that.
The issues facing countries in the Pacific mi ght be similar, whether they be climate
change, the retention of resources, or pollu tion and environmental degradation. It is up
to New Zealand to ensure that we undert ake aid assistance and that development does
not come at the expense of local people, cust oms, and culture. There is a Pacific way,
and it is not wrong. It should be defended. One of those things about the Pacific way is
that their institutions need to be recognised. I have always, for example, believed in the
Great Council of Chiefs in Fiji. They should not be set aside. They should not be, as any
wise nation would understand, an d that goes for the rest of  the Solomons, Vanuatu, and
other places where there is a chiefly role th at the people do respect, and we should seek
to modernise our constitutional approach to understand that. We must look to uphold
and respect the cultural as well as the political boundaries of our neighbours.
There is just one thing I want to say, and that is this: there is a need all over the
world, and that is including in New Zealand, fo r politicians to be seen to be accountable
and transparent. No one is immune from this. I can remember being offshore with a
foreign Minister—I will not say of which country, but it was in the Solomon Islands. He
was berating the local administration. I said to him: “Look, I don’t want to be in the
same room if you’ve forgotten your own history. Don’t you remember the State Bank of
South Australia, Rothwells Bank, or that thre e Premiers in Wester n Australia got done
over under WA Inc.? Do not preach to these people who know about your history. And
I don’t want to be in the room, representing my country, when you do that.”
Back to my point, we need to understand th at accountability and transparency are in
everyone’s interests. I know that there is a Pacific feeling,  because it is very endemic in

items.speaker: Māoridom too. It goes like this
items.text: if you cannot help your own, then who can you help?
And that is the seed of so much nepo tism and corruption, but it is a very, very
understandable cultural phenomenon that we have to, in the interests of the people who
represent us, fight against. It is extraordinarily difficult, because your people expect you
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9563
to have some understanding of the saying “Blood is thicker than water”, but, that said, it
is Government and it is an issue of privilege, and we need to strive against it.
I want to say that increased dialogue between  our countries is of benefit to all. Two
of us were recently at an Australasian Council of Public Accounts Committees meeting
in Australia last week. We f ound it enormously beneficial that Pacific countries were
there and some African countries were ther e, but many of us from Australia and New
Zealand had plenty to learn ourselves. Gathering with representatives from across the
Pacific not only allows for the bettering of relationships and the sharing of ideas but it
also allows for greater scrutiny of how we  are progressing togeth er. For my part, the
New Zealand First Party seriously believes in the Pacific relationship. We believe that is
a special relationship with a capital “S”.
While you are here, you are going to meet all your relations, a nd many are going to
say to you “Which party should we vote for?”. I suggest you say to them: “Well, first of
all, get on the roll, and then vote for the one  party that understands Pacific people—that
party being New Zealand First.” And I can promise you, without any fear of
contradiction, that if you all do that, we will all be better off very soon. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: I know that Pacific people will judge
people by their actions, not their talk. Some years ago I was standing close to a chain
mesh fence at about 10,000 feet in the hi ghlands of Papua New Guinea. The fence
separated people on the outside, who had lived as hunters, gatherers, and gardeners for
more than 5,000 years on that spot. Inside the fence there were fly-in, fly-out foreigners
developing the Porgera Gold Mine, a mine th at cost $300 million to  develop and in the
first 12 months had generated $380 million of income. On one side of the fence were
men, local men, clad in bilums and “arse gra ss”. Miners inside the fence were keeping
the peace, posting 2 kina notes through the holes in the chain mesh. A miner who had
been murdered a week before had caught it on the wrong side of the fence. I overheard
the villagers asking the miners who had given them permission to sit on their land. “The
Government in Port Moresby.”, a miner repl ied. “Wanem disella Govmen e stap long
Moresby?”—“What is this Government in Port Moresby?” That was quite a fair
question in a very remote part of Papua New Guinea without schools, health centres,
electricity, and, in fact, no sign of any Gove rnment at all. I could easily understand why
the villagers in this remote setting ha d no concept of what Papua New Guinea’s
Parliament was at that time. I am sure things have changed.
In Honiara, at 2 o’clock in the morning, I was involved in extracting a former student
of Victoria University, Prim e Minister Bart Ulufa’alu, fr om his office in Parliament,
where he was being held by Malaitans wa nting to overthrow his Government. We
nervously drove him to the house of an expatriate priest for safe keeping, so that at least
he could get a decent night’s sleep and a shower. I was astonished a couple of days later
in a meeting with the overthrowers to be given a faxed letter from the Commonwealth
Parliamentary Association commending th e actions of the MPs involved in the
situation. That was the begi nning of the conflict that sa w the Regional Assistance
Mission to the Solomon Islands (RAMSI) intervention, consuming millions of dollars
that might otherwise have been used fo r core services, which those who elected
politicians expected Parliament to provide.
The underlying dispute between the people of  Malaita and Guadalcanal is land. It
continues to simmer. Solomon Islanders picking apples in my village of Greytown tell
me that the conflict will erupt again as soon as RAMSI departs, and that will not help
anybody. Land ownership was central to the pr oblem on Bougainville. It took 10 years
to resolve, but it took us 8 years to lear n that we needed to  stop trying to take
responsibility for others’ problems and to  instead support communities to take
responsibility for resolving their own disputes. Although rarely acknowledged, M āori
9564 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
process was critical to the resolution of the issue between Papua New Guinea and
Bougainville. That took place mainly on Ma takana Island. The people of the Solomon
Islands may yet find those lessons learnt in Bougainville to be useful.
Cohesion across the Pacific Islands Foru m members has loosened since leaders
around that time of decolonisation—the great t ōtara trees Ratu Mara, Albert Henry,
Michael Somare, Robert Rex, Bob Hawke, and Hammer DeRoburt—worked together to
unite the region. Since their time we have, perhaps unwittingly, devolved leaderships to
public servants. I think of last year’s Forum Economic Ministers’ Meeting, which I
went to. There were about 10 Mi nisters there, with at leas t 70 officials in attendance.
The officials spent 2 days before we arrived, and the whole time we were there, meeting
and constructing an 84-paragraph communiqué, which no one has read since. That is not
leadership. I hope that any record of this meeting will be no longer than two sides of
one A4 page.
Time pressures and fast planes have reduced the time that leaders spend together,
reducing their engagement with each other.  We do not know each other as well as we
used to. This meeting is trying to help ove rcome this sort of problem with the next
generation of leaders sitting in our gallery. Th is meeting, I hope, will help us to get to
know each other much better, because it is much easier to work with people you know
and understand.
Recent months have seen the emergence of new entities like the Melanesian
spearhead group based in Vanuatu, the Microne sian leaders’ forum based in Guam, and
the beginning of a Polynesian leaders’ group coalescing around Samoa. Participants
from 22 countries were invited to this foru m. Never before has this Parliament House
seen the sort of group we have in it today. Never in the history of our region have so
many politicians and leaders gathered under one roof in the Pacific to meet, share ideas,
and get to know one another. My committee,  the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee, hopes that this gath ering will rejuvena te our ability to work together as
brothers and sisters bound t ogether by our great Pacific Ocean. We hope that working
more closely together will help our region to work more collaboratively for the
betterment of those we represent. The ocean that touches all of your shores encircles our
country too. Irrespective of our language or our culture, we are all Pacific people in this
House today. The future well-being of your community is tied to mine. We are joined
together like a plaited rope.
Meetings like this do not happen by accide nt, and a huge number of people have
worked for this outcome. My one-time boss and hugely supportive friend Mike Moore
championed the idea of a Pacific leadership congress in his book A Pacific Parliament.
We would not be gathered here without the support of Prime Minister Key. I bring
greetings from our Minister of  Foreign Affairs, Murray McCully, and I want to thank
him because it was his involvement and support th at provided the help for us to be here
today. He has asked me to convey his greeti ngs to you from Africa, where he is on a 2-
week assignment lobbying hard for New Zeal and’s bid for the seat on the United
Nations Security Council. I have to say to th e House that we actually had one hell of an
argument before he took off because he really  wanted to be here, but we could not slot
this meeting in between the energy conferen ce and other things going on in the region.
So in the finish he lost, and I am grateful to him for doing that.
I want to thank David Carter, our Speaker; Mary Harris, Clerk of the Parliament; and
Lesley Ferguson and her team for the huge support. And thank you to each one of our
parliamentary colleagues fo r the support you have extende d. Of course, none of us
would be here without my girls: Emily Tayl forth and Morag Santini. They have worked
huge hours. They are just magnificent.
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9565
It is New Zealand’s respons ibility to work collaborati vely with each of you as
neighbours and friends. Understanding each othe r and working together is essential to
the growth and development of the communitie s we represent. Any instability in our
neighbourhood has consequences for us all. Stable and affordable governance is an
essential precondition for economic growth. New Zealand is sma ller than Sydney, and
Sydney does not maintain an army, a navy, an  air force, and 50 diplomatic officers
offshore. We all struggle to maintain an affordable Government. The bigger it is, the
more constraints there are on those who are in our busin ess sector creating jobs.
Keeping bureaucracy at a size our communities  can afford is critical to sustainable
growth and creating jobs for our young peopl e. Our geography dictat es a high level of
interdependence logistically and economically in this region.
Finally, I would like to welcome especial ly our friends from the North-west
Pacific—Guam, Palau, the Marshalls, American Samoa, the Marianas, and the
Federated States of Micronesia. Pacific people contribute to New Zealand at every
level—in our universities, in our Parliament, in our factories, and in our Government
departments. We are a South Pacific nation. This is deep in our DNA. New Zealand
politicians no longer visit the Pacific only on the way to London. Our strategic
ambitions are transparent. We want to see the island countries of the North-west Pacific
integrated into the institutions of the Sout h Pacific, because it makes sense and because
it makes us stronger. That is why our Minister of Foreign A ffairs made great efforts to
encourage you all to participate in the Pa cific Islands Forum, the premier political
meeting in our region. That is why our Minist er has visited the Marshall Islands, which
will host the next forum.
We have common problems. We can, theref ore, have common so lutions. This is
what this historic assembly is about. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: To the delegates w ho are gathered here,
from more than 18 countries across the Pa cific, a warm welcome to Aotearoa New
Zealand. The waters of the Pacific lap the shores of all of our  countries and bring
together our peoples from diverse ethnicities , cultures, and languages. All of us, with
the exception of maybe the bi g island to the west of New Zealand, are small island
States facing the challenges of remoteness a nd a lack of economies of scale. We know
that we can better meet those challenges wo rking together rather  than as separate
countries, and that is why we are gathered here this weekend to look at those challenges,
to work together, to learn from each other, to  talk together, and to find solutions that
will make life better for all of the peoples of the Pacific.
Our countries share not only our Pacific lo cation but also the bonds of history, of
culture, of family, and of tr ade. You have already heard that this country was first
shaped by people from the Pacific a mille nnium ago—the tangata whenua of this
country, the Māori people. Then it was shaped by the Europeans, from whom we gained
many of our institutions.
We are being influenced today by other dive rse ethnicities from As ia, but I want to
pay particular tribute to those who came to our country from the Pacific 50 and 60 years
ago and ever since, because it is the migrati on from the Pacific that has helped shaped
the identity that we have as New Zealande rs, which is different from other countries
from which we draw our heritage. I want to thank the peoples of the Pacific for the hard
work that they put into building our country and our economy, and for the huge
contribution that they make on the sporting fi elds of New Zealand and to the culture of
this country that enriches us and makes us stronger.
The Pacific is the area where New Zealand, as a small country, can make the greatest
difference, and where we can make the greate st contribution. That is why I am pleased
that well over half of the de velopment assistance that we can provide goes directly to
9566 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
the Pacific. But there are other things that we  can do, as well. One of the initiatives that
we worked on when I was in Government  was the Recognised Seasonal Employer
scheme, a scheme that is of real benefit to New Zealand but also to the people from your
countries because it provides work and it prov ides resources that they can take back to
their families and their communities.
But there are other things, as  well, and I want to pay sp ecial tribute to our Defence
Force and our police force. In both of thos e forces, we see the marked influence of
Māori members and Pasifika members. Those fo rces have helped at times of natural
disasters, such as the tsunami and the cyclones. They have helped to protect our
resources, the fishery resources—and I sa y “our”, meaning the resources of the
Pacific—from those from other countries w ho would plunder it. They have helped in
search and rescue, and I want to pay particular credit to them for the work that they have
done in places like the Solomons and in Tonga , and in Timor-Leste—i f I class that as
part of the Pacific—in peacekeeping. The partic ular tribute I pay to our forces is that
they regard themselves as equals with the people where they serve overseas.
I want to make another special  tribute, and that is to the defence force that we used,
as a Government, from the 1970s to run our flag up and protest ag ainst the people from
the United States, from Britain, from Fran ce, and elsewhere who tested their dirty
nuclear weapons in our Pacific Ocean. We ha ve fought together, alongside each other,
