as Pacific nations to bring a Pacific that is finally free of nuclear weapon testing but,
sadly, not free of the consequences, the pollution, that those things caused.
The Pacific faces huge challenges—economi cally, socially, environmentally, and
politically. But we should not be daunted by our problems; we should be inspired and
motivated by what we can make of the Paci fic, as the most beautiful region in the
world. In 2011 when the forum leaders met in  Auckland, they talked about their vision
for the Pacific—the Pacific as a region of peace and harmony, security, and economic
prosperity, the Pacific where people could lead free and worthwhile lives, a place where
we could celebrate together our diversity, a nd value the cultures, the traditions, and the
religious beliefs of all.
The forum sets some ambitions for us in th e Pacific, that we should become a region
respected for the quality of our governance, where we should be respected for the
sustainable management of our resources a nd our environment, where we should fully
observe democratic values and be respecte d for the defence and promotion of human
rights. We fall short of that vision, but we should be inspired and we should be
motivated in the days ahead to work out ways to make that vision the reality for our
place in the Pacific, to create an environment that is sound and sustainable.
Two of the areas where we have the greates t comparative advantage are in fisheries
and in tourism. Both rely on the proper management of our environment. I am also
conscious that it is the small islands of the Pacific that do little to cause the problem of
global warming but, as countries, will be the firs t victims of that process. I have been in
Tuvalu and I have been in the Marshall Is lands where the leaders of those countries
have said to me “Frankly, our people could be come the first environmental refugees in
the world.” It is beholden on countries lik e New Zealand and Australia to not oppose
the stand that the Pacific takes to stop the process of global warming but to get
alongside the Pacific to work with and support the Pacific in those objectives.
I want to talk also about de velopment in the Pacific that benefits not simply the elite
but all of the people. Our goal in developm ent assistance as a Government was to
eliminate poverty. It covered many areas. The Government today talks about sustainable
economic development. That is an important goal, but it is not th e only goal, and we
need to ensure that in the process of supporting sustai nable economic development, the
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9567
benefits of that development go to the peopl e as a whole and not simply to those who
already control wealth and power.
I want to talk about trading relationship s, because I have worked on deals for the
Pacific Island Countries Trade Agreemen t and the Pacific Agreement on Closer
Economic Relations, and I want to make this commitment. They are trading
arrangements that must work for mutual benefit and must also address the huge
imbalances in trade between our countries. We  must give back to the Pacific, because
we take so much from it in terms of trade.
I want to talk, finally, about the role that strong democracy and good governance can
play. We need not necessarily a Westminste r model—that might not be the particular
model of democracy for the Pacific. It ma y be something that embeds better in your
local culture and traditions. But whatever m odel is used, the basi c foundation stones of
democracy must be supported and enhanced—openness and transparency—because that
is how you deal with the pr oblems of corruption. We need  honesty. We need integrity.
We do not need self-serving corruption. We need a free me dia in every one of our
countries—not media subject to censorship. We need the rule of law—where no New
Zealander and no person in the Pacific is above the law. In our country a Prime Minister
was taken to task for speeding in a police convoy. Many people in the world regard that
as odd, but it was a sign that New Zeala nders say that everybody is under the law
regardless of the circumstances.
We also need to acknowledge the role of political parties not set out in constitutions,
which is that they are the glue that holds the system together to make it work properly,
and also the legitimate role of opposition.
There is much that we will talk about in the coming days. Once again, welcome to
our country. It is good to have you here. You are our closest friends and we look
forward to working together with you. Thank you very much.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : Fa‘afetai lava.
Fakauelahi. Meitaki maata. Fa‘atalofa atu, malo le soifua ma le lagi e mama I le pa‘ia
ma le mamalu o le maota fono aemaise le au -vala‘aulia. Kia orana. Ia orana. Talofa
koutou. Taloha ni. Malo ni. Fakaalofa lahi at u. Kam na Mauri. Alo. Halo ola keta. Kia
ora tātou katoa. And, of course, warm Pacific greetings.
Life is a dream for the wise, a game for the fool—and there are many of them in
some parts of the House—a comedy for the rich, and a tragedy for the poor, who are
struggling with the un employment rates in our country right now. It is wonderful to
have our families, our friends, and our peopl e from the Pacific here today. Afio mai,
maliu mai, welcome.
Let me start by saying that parliamentarians  in the Pacific region must ensure that
their policy machinery is going to benefit the local communities—the ones who matter,
the people. The Pacific Parliamentary and Political Leaders Forum, which New Zealand
is hosting this weekend, is a pe rfect platform for us to ex change experiences and learn
from each other. It is also a chance where we can exchange expert knowledge that will
assist in eliminating barriers that continue to prevent leadership in the Pacific region
from making progress. Good leadership, gove rnance, and democracy are essential for
enabling people to live enjoyable lives in th e Pacific. There is a need—not a want—to
emphasise the importance of participative democracy and how this will contribute to the
strengthening of our economic, social, and political development.
Regional development, benefiting from the Pacific plan and strategies, will require a
more inclusive network that is well info rmed and open to diffe rent viewpoints that
traditionally might have been ignored. There needs to be a shift in our mentality from
leadership that is biased and tainted by exclusionary norms. Civil society has a vital role
to play in ensuring that political leadership  and credibility are held accountable for the
9568 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
policies and strategies that are put in place. People in local communities need to be kept
in the know and also afforded the platform to engage in dialogue and discussions on
matters that affect them. The Pacific plan is everyone’s business and it is paramount that
all stakeholders concerned—that is, all of us —are able to voice their concerns and add
more value and weight to the issues that directly affect them.
As people of the Pacific we realise that our  mistrust of the future makes it hard to
give up the past. As Pacific people, history has taught us many lessons that we will not
forget. In some respects we have been more fortunate than others. Many Pacific Islands
were colonised in a time when the “great power s” realised that they had a responsibility
not only to take but also to  give back. I look at my ow n country of origin and the
periods of colonisation, firstly, under Germany, and then under the New Zealand
administration. Inevitably, these administratio ns brought misery and hardship to many
Samoans. However, they also brought infras tructure, roads, school s, power, hospitals,
transportation, telecommunicati on, trade, and more. It enab led many of our people to
step into the global village with some conf idence, as our forefathers looked beyond the
shores of our many islands, as they saw at that time an opportunity to better themselves
and their children.
Most Pacific people understand that thei r special relationships with both New
Zealand and Australia are something that s hould be valued and maintained. We have
seen the economic expansion and influen ce of our Asian neighbours. We can only look
on in awe in recent years as these economic gi ants spread their hands across the Pacific.
Successive New Zealand Govern ments are beginning to unders tand that they can no
longer take their nearest nei ghbours for granted if we ar e to maintain our unique
strategic, economic, and cultural ties. I fully understand why France and the United
States take their Pacific protectorates very, very seriously. In a modern world the islands
of the Pacific have a unique opportunity to s upply not only, as in the past, New Zealand
and Australia with the labour  force, but also a nearby warm and welcoming holiday
destination. Our Pacific neighbours are in a special position that gives the opportunity to
take the best of the West and the East  and maintain the unique friendships and
relationships that have developed over many years. If New Zealand fails to recognise
and support the importance of their position in our world, then we undoubtedly lose
much of the unique character that makes our New Zealand and our Pacific neighbours a
special, unique, place in our global village.
One of the main issues that is confronting the Pacific region is equality. Participative
democracy and women go hand in hand with go vernance, and, given th at I am the only
Pacific Island woman in Parliament this te rm and also the first woman MP born outside
of New Zealand, I think I have every right to  advocate for this particular topic to be
discussed in this House. [ Interruption] I hear that Michael Woodward would like to
correct something that I have said.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: Yes, my name: Woodhouse.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR: Woodhouse.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: But, also, Melissa Lee was born outside New Zealand.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : I happen to be referring to the
Pacific, Michael Woodhouse. Thank you.
It allows the process of democracy to fully capture a nation’s development needs and
solutions to these needs. For years now women have been left firmly at the margins and
have been excluded from sitting in on decision -making processes. Or, if they are, they
have little room to manoeuvre themselves because political authority is still very much a
man’s world. We fail to realise that women ma ke up half of the Pacific population. This
is why their perspective and active participation is essential for good governance and for
the process of democracy. Collectivel y, women make up 12 percent of the
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9569
parliamentary seats in the Pacific Islands, and if we exclude the French territories, that
figure would fall to a mere 5 percent. New Zeal and has a responsibility to play a role in
this area, although it does not help that there are budget cuts at the Ministry of Foreign
Affairs and Trade at the moment. Participation should be viewed as a measure by which
we can assess good governance. This will ensure  that the process of democracy is not
tainted and that political credibility is, in fact, credible. Thank you.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Kia orana tatou katoatoa e te aroa matua o te atua
matou. Greetings to everyone here. Kia oran a tatou katoatoa te moana nui a kiwa.
Greetings to all our Pasifika visitors and guests who are he re today. You have travelled
from far away to be with us at this ina ugural parliamentary foru m and to listen to and
observe this historic debate of  3 hours. It is the first one th at has ever been held in the
House to discuss our Pacific issues. Not only is it historic but you r presence here is
historic, as well. So we do look forward to th e next 3 days and spending time to debate
and to discuss important issues, as well.
I want to just reflect on  a story that I once heard. There was a young Pasifika man
and a young European man—a Palagi, a Papa’a—and together they were friends. They
decided to go off, and they wanted to go camping. So they went camping. They did not
have a tent, but what they di d have was a blue tarpaulin from The Warehouse. So they
put the blue tarpaulin up over the top. They put this tarpaulin up and said: “That will be
our tent.” They went out and they played for some time, and eventually they stopped
and had something to eat. They had some povi masima, some corned beef, which is
very healthy for you. They had some kalo a nd then had some breadfruit. They sat and
they ate, and they told all the stories about how their parents would be really annoyed
that they had spent this night out in the tent.
Anyway, they went to sleep, and in the middle of the night, the Palagi—the young
Papa’a man—sort of motioned to the young Pa sifika man and he said: “Hey, hey, hey,
get up.” The young Pasifika man said: “What’s wrong?”, and the young Palagi man
said: “Look up. Look up, and what do you see?”. Then the young Pasifika man said:
“What do you mean?”, and the Pa lagi said: “Well, what I s ee when I look up is that I
think about astrological. That means that I learnt at school about the wonderful things
about the stars and the Milky Way, and isn’t it wonderful?”. And the Pasifika man said:
“When I look up I think about astronomical, as well”—oh, I have got them mixed up,
actually. Astrological  is about magazines and read ing about your horoscopes, and
astronomical is about the Milky Way and the stars.
Then the young Pasifika man wanted to say so mething, but that is not all because the
Palagi boy was on a roll, you see. He was brigh t; he was intelligent.  He said: “I think
about theological, and I think about when we went to chur ch and they taught us about
how God had created this wonderful universe an d this world.” Then he said: “But that’s
not all. I think about meteorol ogical, and I think about the f act that I look up and I see
those stars, and their movement is telling me  that tomorrow is going to be a fine day.”
With that he had finished. Then he moti oned to his young Pasifika friend and he said:
“So what do you see when you look up?”. The young Pasifika man looked up and
looked to his Palagi friend and said: “Someone stole our tent.”
Here is a very simple analogy and a very interesting story. In other words, you can
have a world of intelligence, you can have development, you can have economic, social,
and cultural development, but at the same time too, if we are not careful, we can miss
the very thing that is important to us. So can I encourage all of us, both the politicians
here and the political leaders who are here  today, to sometimes stop for a moment to
look up and see and have a little common sense.
That is what the debates over the next 2 to 3 days are actually going to be about. You
see, we can be intelligent, we can have research, we can have evidence—and those
9570 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
things are absolutely important—but you and I know that in the co mmunities that we
live in, whether here in Aotearoa New Z ealand or back home in your communities,
sometimes the issues are actually about having some common sense.
I believe that what our communities are looking for is leaders who have a little
common sense and who speak in a language th at they understand, that they can connect
with, and with whom they can communicate b ack to you and me. That is what they are
looking for and that is the confidence that they are asking for in us, as well.
I want to add a simple littl e story about taxi drivers. Taxis are wonderful things—we
politicians over here in New Zealand travel in taxis all the time. I was travelling over to
Wellington Airport on my way up to the promised land of Auckland, and, as I was
doing that, I had a conversation with the taxi driv er, and this is what he said. He said to
me: “So how’s it been going? Going well?”. I sa id: “There are some difficult issues in
New Zealand that we are having to deal wi th.” He was an Englishman, and he simply
said this to me: “Do you guys realise that you are just a pimple on the backside of the
world?”. I said: “What! What do you mea n, a pimple on the backside—how long have
you been here?”, and I ardently advocat ed and spoke very strongly about how
wonderful New Zealand is. After about 5 minut es he then said: “S orry, sorry, I stand
corrected. You are a very nice pimple on the backside of the world.”
It is really interesting, because in one sense, even though this was a funny sort of
story, there was some truth, in a sense, about  the size and scale of who we are and to
whom we belong. See, in one sense, to th e bigger parts of the world we are simply
smaller than the rest of the other parts of the world. Why would anyone be interested in
who we are or in what we have to contribut e? That is a very in teresting question we
need to ask, but at the same time too, they are still knocking on our doors.
I wanted to say that, because I think that is one of the thi ngs that we have to contend
with in our discussions and in our debate. De spite the size and the scale of who we are,
we have to ask the question: what is our point  of difference that we have to offer, both
here in New Zealand and also  out in the region? When we know what our point of
difference is, then that is what we take to the bargaining table of trade agreements and
of economic development out there in the rest of the world.
You see, the old man who was interviewe d by a reporter was asked this: “You come
from the smallest nation in the world?”, a nd his reply was this: “No, sir, I come from
the biggest ocean in the world.” What a confident reply, only because of this: he knew
who he was. He knew what he was contribu ting and he knew where he came from. Can
I say to us and to our Pasifika people that we have to absolutely know not only who we
are and to whom we belong but also what it is  that we contribute to the rest of the
world. We need to be confident—as the old man said: “I come from the biggest ocean in
the world.” Why? Because there was once a history that was told about us that said that
we were idle navigators—we were the people who somehow idled around the world and
found these little islands in the vastness of the Pacific— and yet that has now been
proven to be wrong in that we were conscious , we were confident, and we were capable
travellers and navigators of the whole of the Pacific.
We were navigators for the rest of the world. We inhabited th e very islands that
people had written about. So when the pe ople from Europe, when the people from
England, and the people from other places came, whom did they find? They found
Polynesian Pasifika people in habiting those islands with a civilisation and with the
confidence of who they were and what they could contribute. We need to have that
confidence.

items.speaker: Can I say to us this
items.text: we ar e political navigators. Our people and our community need
us. They need us to be conscious of the currents of the world that are around us. We
need to know what political opinion is around,  but at the same time too we need to
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9571
know the mood of our people. How well do we know our communities? How well do
we connect with our people? You see, it is very easy for us in a position of power and of
influence to sometimes be in a place of an ivory tower. In other words, we can become
disconnected—we can become disconnected. So th ese are the things that are absolutely
important to who we are as leaders and as political navigators.
That is the task that you have . That is the task that I ha ve. You and I are similar in a
number of senses. I am a new MP. I am the fi rst Kiwi of Cook Island descent to be here
in this New Zealand Parliament. I am only here today because I had my grandmother
and I had my family and the people around me who supported me to be here. Because of
that I have a sense of accountability and responsibility back to them.
Today I do not want to talk rhetoric about the amount of contribution that we have to
make, because others will talk about that. I want to make a passionate plea to you who
are here today, and to me, for this one thing—we will debate for 3 days about the issues.
For the first time we are doing this. We are stopping and we are saying this is our space.
Sometimes we need the Palagis and the Papa ’as to be outside the room. No, they will
not be, because they will actually be inside here with us, but sometimes we need to have
the outsiders out of the room. And here is the reason why. It is because we need to
discuss our issues. What we also need to say is this: what are we going to take
responsibility for? Yes, we have had aid for many years. Yes, we have had people
supporting our development, but when are we  going to take responsibility? When are
we going to find our own sustainability?
There comes a time when we need to say, both domestically here in New Zealand
and to our own Pasifika communities, that we are outraged when people use our
communities to stroke a charitable ego and when they refer to the poverty of our
nations. We came here. Our people know what pove rty smells like, tastes like, and they
have lived it. But, guess what? We do not see it as poverty. Let us turn what other
people see as a negative into a positive about what we have  as a people. We have so
much to contribute to this nation. We have so much to contribute in our passion. We are
more than just sporting people. We are more  than just performers and dancers on a
stage. We have intelligence. Let us call back the intelligence that comes from the
navigators of the past. Let us stand confidently and contribute not only to New Zealand
but to the Pacific and to whoever else comes.
I am proud to be in this place today to speak to the leaders that are here today and to
our Pasifika community. We have a pride of  place in this country, in this region, and
today is our day. Thank you.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): May I quickly acknowledge our many
distinguished visitors, parliamentarians, and political leaders of the South Pacific Island
countries who are present today. Ou te fa‘apoi poi lili‘a fa‘aalofisa o tupu nai le Malae o
Vavau ma o‘u fa‘atulouna le paia maualuga ua aofaga potopoto, tulou, tulou, tulouna ia.
I acknowledge the participants from Amer ican Samoa, Cook Islands, the Federated
States of Micronesia, Fiji, Guam, Kiribati,  the Republic of the Marshall Islands, New
Caledonia, Niue, the Commonwealth of the Northern  Mariana Islands, Palau, Papua
New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tokelau, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.
Welcome, once again, to all the participants  from these countries to New Zealand’s
House of Representatives. I feel that this is a momentous occasion, especially for those
of us in this Parliament who have strong Pacific Island links back to the homeland, and
there are also members of Parliament he re who represent pockets of the Pacific
community who live here in Aotearoa New Zealand.
It feels, with the presence of so many fr om the Pacific Island nations, that, truly, the
Pacific is in the House. W ho would have thought that su ch a thing would be possible
when our Pacific parents, some of the first arrivals, came to New Zealand all those years
9572 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
ago? Who would have thought that for the first time in the history of our nations, such a
diverse group of political leaders from the Pacific outside the Pacific Island Forum
would sit shoulder to shoulder with New Zealand members of Parliament? It will be the
first time that such a large and diverse gr oup of foreign parliamentarians will have the
opportunity, as they will have today, tomorrow, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday, to be
able to speak in the debati ng chamber of New Zealand’s Pa rliament. That is usually
reserved and extended only to visiting lead ers of significance, and I acknowledge each
and every one of you as leaders of significance.
For myself, and I suspect the feeling will be shared by all members of this House,
our gathering in the next few days, from a New Zealand perspective, is a big deal. For
me, as a Labour MP, it was a big deal when the Labour Government initiated the
Inquiry into New Zealand’s relationship with South Pacific countries. From that inquiry
emerged the idea for this forum. I acknowle dge my former parliamentary colleagues
who are no longer with us in this House, the Hon Luamanuvao Winnie Laban and the
Hon Vui Mark Gosche, who were part of th e Labour Government that initiated this
inquiry in 2006. I also acknowledge and tha nk the National Government, which picked
up this inquiry and completed the work in December 2010.
I acknowledge and pay tribute to the multip artisan way in which all parties from
across the political spectrum of this House have put their shoulder behind making this
forum a reality. I want to thank, in particul ar, Mr John Hayes, the chair of the Foreign
Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, for his efforts and drive. I suspect that he, most
of all of the committee members today, cannot wa it for this forum to be over. I want to
thank also the many members of that committ ee, past and present, for their work and
commitment to the Pacific region and for bringing everybody together.
In the next few days the Pacific leaders and members in this House will debate a
range of issues, and these issues, which I will raise briefly, are the issues that the
members or the delegates themselves have forwarded. They include gender equality.
There is a strong debate throughout Ne w Zealand about having more women
representatives in this particular House. I note also that that is the challenge facing
many throughout the Pacific countries.
The media—like it or not, sometimes we cr ave media attention, and then there are
other times when we wish we did not have so much media attention. Like it or not, in
the work we are involved with, the media, as  far as New Zealand is concerned, have a
critical role to play in our democracy.
The environment and climate change—I agree, it is an issue that has an impact, and I
have seen the impact of rising sea water levels. As a member of the committee, and as a
representative of the Labour Party, I have had the privilege of visiting, with many of our
other colleagues, some of our Pacific Island s. I am saddened when I see some islands,
where I think to myself that perhaps it might  take only a wave to sweep over them and
there would be no more island. So I think that that is a critical issue in our debates.
Delivering for local communities is not only an issue that you face but we certainly
have our own challenges here. Health care is  a big one, because that has to do with the
health and safety of the next generati on. Business development and job creation—you
will have noted some of the debates in the la st few days about our call for better-quality
jobs and high-paying jobs. Then there is the global economic outlook and opportunities
for this region. I suppose, for the sins of the committee, we have also included
discussions around sports and rugby.
The report of the 2006 inquiry reflected the st rong feeling that most Kiwis have that
New Zealand has a special relationship with  the people of the Pacific, both in New
Zealand and in the South Pacific region. Our ties to the Pacific are many and varied. I
think that Samoa’s head of State, His Highness Tuiatua Tupua Tamasese Efi, summed
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9573
this feeling up best for me when he tha nked New Zealand for supporting Samoa after
the 2009 tsunami. He said: “He who comes to my aid is kin.” This feeling of kinship
and connectedness with the Pacific is a good foundation for further strengthening New
Zealand’s relationships with those of you w ho are, and who will become, future leaders
of your parliaments in the Pacific.
This forum expands our relations with the Pa cific leaders by setting aside a week of
the New Zealand Parliament’s time to host an d focus not only on i ssues of concern to
the domestic, Pacific neighbourhood but also on issues of common regional interest.
Members of the New Zealand public who ha d the opportunity to make submissions on
the 2006 inquiry also saw scope for New Zeal and to make better use of the knowledge
and expertise of Pacific people residing in  New Zealand, particularly regarding the
provision of services to Pacific people and the aid programme. Many Pacific people
living in New Zealand have strong links w ith, and an understandi ng of, the culture,
values, and aspirations of Pacific communities. They represent an underutilised asset on
which New Zealand could capitalise. For this reason, the committee has organised many
of the events and seminars to include as mu ch as possible of the talents and expertise
that is available within our Pacific region.
Earlier—I will finish this off, as time is running out—the Minister for Pacific Island
Affairs made reference to the growing Pacific population here in Aotearoa New
Zealand. I suspect, however, that the basis for that reference was the 2006 census, and
we have not had another census recently, not  until last month. So I think the figure for
the Pacific population may be smaller—some  of us will have had more children
between 2006 and the census last month. That proposes some exciting elements for the
future of Aotearoa New Zealand, because we  have not only one of  the fastest-growing
populations but also one of the youngest populations.
I continually promote that population as young , beautiful, and gifted, and I use that
statement to challenge them to look to the fu ture of Aotearoa New Zealand and to plant
their feet firmly here, as this is their home . But by giving them that  challenge, that also
offers up challenges for the Pacific Island region. The longer we are here, the firmer our
feet are planted in Aotearoa New Zealand and the weaker the links are back to our
homelands, and that also will have ramificatio ns for those countries that are reliant on
the remittances that come from Aotearoa New Zealand.
May I conclude by saying that my collea gues have raised many other issues. In
addition to the issues that are on our progra mme, I would hope that we also explore the
opportunities to find the space to look at other issues that we can talk about, in the hope
that we will develop a greater and better vision for the future. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Ou te fa’atulou atu i le paia
o le fono fai tulafono. Le Palemene o le malo o Niu Sila. Le paia maualuga le afio o le
Kovaga sili. Le afio le afioga le Palemia. Le mamalu le Kapeneta. Le afio lau afioga le
Fofoga Fetalai. Le paia tele o sui usufono ma i malo eseese. Le Pasefika ae tainane. Le
paia maualuga le sui usufono o le Palemene o Aotearoa, Niu Sila. Tulou, Tulou, Tulou
lava. O le a ou tautala i le gagana e fa’asino i ai lenei aso.
Mr Assistant Speaker, I have greeted you in my native tongue of Samoan, and I greet
members of this House, members of Cabinet,  of course, and the Prime Minister, and I
want to especially welcome the delegates to the Pacific Parliamentary and Political
Leaders Forum. Delegates, I want to thank you personally for venturing here for a week
from your valuable family time, work commitments, and other duties and obligations. It
is an honour to speak in this debate, firs tly, as a Pacific pers on representing the many
Pacific people in this Parliament and across this country, as well as  the fine people of
Maungakiekie in Auckland; and, secondly, as  a Pacific person bor n in Samoa whose
family came here seeking a better life. Like  many of you in the gallery, we came as
9574 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
migrants here many years ago. My parents wa nted a better life for my siblings and
me—a better education, well-paying jobs, to ultimately serve our families and our
communities. Finally, I am honoured to be a member of this John Key - led National
Government, and we are committed to the pli ght of not just Pacific people here in
Aotearoa New Zealand but also our Pacific brothers and sisters who are scattered across
the many Pacific Islands across the Pacific Ocean.
I, like my colleagues, would like to thank the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee for bringing about this forum. This  forum is a consequence of its report to
Parliament in 2010. I commend the leadership of John Hayes and the recommendation
to foster better relationships with parliamentarians across the Pacific. This was
something that was shared with me in my experiences when I visited the Pacific on the
many Pacific missions that we go on as parliamentarians here in New Zealand.
I think it is significant that New Zealand is  hosting this forum, and it demonstrates
New Zealand’s leading role in the Pacific, in which we punch well above our weight in
terms of contributions that we make to our Pacific nations. To that end, we have heard
how we spend over $250 million annually in aid to the Pacific. Of course, that is more
than half of our aid budget, and I would like to thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs,
the Hon Murray McCully, who is not here, because he steadfastly increased our
commitment of these resources so that we may improve the plight of Pacific people in
the Pacific. Of course, this aid includes  $145 million in funding towards a joint venture
with Australia, and that will provide over half a million children with education across
the Pacific. We have heard domestically that  we are assisting Pacific workers with the
Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme. This provides $25 million in take-home pay,
much of which is returned to the Pacific.
Indeed, only last month, we have heard, we hosted in Auckland the Pacific Energy
Summit, where we managed to secure donor commitments of $635 million. These funds
are to advance renewable energy projects and energy efficiency plans. All these projects
do not even go towards some of the other ar eas that have been mentioned already, and
they include New Zealand aid projects th at focus on non-communi cable diseases and
sexual and reproductive health, as well as strengthening na tional health systems, which
we will be hearing about later in our forum.
Of course, relationships are not just a bout aid funding. We are here to build on
relationships, foster cooperation, and prom ote political cohesion across our Pacific
boundaries. We will be discussing issues such  as health, climate change, and gender
issues. However, there is little  time and much to discuss, so  my hope is that other items
may find themselves on the agenda during th e breaks, during the rugby, and during the
barbecue tonight at Premier House. Some of these subjects include education, economic
development, infrastructure, and employment matters. I believe that these matters are
interconnected, and that education still remains—we have the education Minister, Hekia
Parata, here with us today—the  key to unlocking the potent ial of our Pacific peoples,
both here in New Zealand and across the Pacific.
These are some of the issues that I have been pushing for Pacific people in Aotearoa
New Zealand. Therefore, these are the issues  I am interested in hearing from you, our
delegates, about. I know how much we have  to learn from your experiences in the
Pacific, your unique Pacific knowledge a nd wisdom, and how we can apply those
experiences to Aotearoa New Zealand. I know  that sustainable economic development
cannot happen in an environment where basi c education is weak, so I would hope that
discussions include how we can assist in  building models for infrastructure and
education. What are effective ways of pr oviding education services and developing a
modern workforce to sustain t hose higher standards in the Paci fic? What is the role of
the internet in leveraging the learning of kids in the Pacific? As you can see, delegates, I
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9575
have more questions than answers for you, but  I am certainly here to listen and learn
from your experiences in the Pacific.
I would like to use a local example of a pr oject called Manaiakalani. This project has
assisted young Pacific and M āori children through wireless networks and affordable
netbooks. I know those types of learning models are possible—in fact, they are probably
happening in the Pacific—and I would like to hear from you, delegates, during the
weekend on this. In terms of  infrastructure—apart from the constraints around funding,
which we all debate and we all disagree upon across this House—we must ask how a
project is delivered such that it is sensitive to Pacific cultural values, our traditions, and
our norms, while creating opportunities for em ployment and wealth creation. Those are
just some of the things that  we grapple with here, and I would like to hear from you,
delegates, as to how you deal with them in your nations. May I say that we need to hear
your voices in this engagement so that we may better understand  how we can engage
with you, our Pacific neighbours, and how we can improve the lives of your people as
you can do for the lives of our people here in New Zealand.
When we consider issues of economic deve lopment, we need to assess issues of
trade. The Pacific, of course, has offered mu ch in the way of trade to New Zealand. We
have nearly $1 billion annually  and it is New Zealand’s se venth-largest export market
and our 20 th-largest trading market. Herein lies th e interesting issue, because although
we benefit greatly from exports to the Pacifi c, the surplus does not necessarily benefit
our Pacific neighbours. Although we all accep t that volume of trade is important
because it raises all our sta ndards of living, we know only too well that extremely large
balance of trade deficits can be crippli ng to countries, leading to high levels of
Government debt and/or the sale of domestic assets. That is something for you to
ponder this weekend, and I again urge you to give us some feedback on that.
So the question is how we can foster domes tic industries that lead to greater exports,
not just to New Zealand but more global market s. To that end I have raised in select
committee financial reviews here in New Z ealand how we can assist you with those
markets. What can New Zealand Trade and Enterprise do to assist in those markets with
introductions to buyers of your goods and services? For the delegates, please assist us in
how we can address what I believe is a precarious anomaly. But trade is about
relationships in foreign lands, and can prove expensive, distant, and out of reach for
Pacific traders. Again, delegates, I challenge you that intra-Pacific trade, between your
countries, as well as between New Zealand and your countries, is particularly important.
I also urge you to think about markets of va lue that many of your nations have strong
links to—for example, the United States, Aust ralia, and, of course, of late, China. We
have also had the Pacific Cooperation F oundation in New Zeala nd, which is a public-
private organisation that leverages a lot of those promotions to trade.
Finally, may I commend to you the work of the annual Pacific Islands Forum, which
brings together leaders from 15 Pacific nations. This forum, I believe, complements that
work. I look forward to working with you in  this forum to suppor t our already strong
relationships between our nations. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: This is a split call of 5 minutes, Kris Faafoi.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Yes, and I will be sharing it with my Fijian
brother Rajen Prasad. Mr Deputy Speaker, ta loha ni, and to the delegation from the
Pacific, taloha ni. It is a privilege to speak in this debate.
As one of the five Pacific members of this  Parliament, this House of Representatives
welcomes you. This forum will begin and stre ngthen strong personal and national links.
As Labour leader, David Shearer, put it, we wi ll get to know each other better. I would
like to acknowledge my fellow Pacific MPs in  this House: my colleague Su’a William
Sio, Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, Alfred Ngaro, and Asenati Lole-Taylor. As you will see, our
9576 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
Pacific representation is pan-pol itical. We are diverse not only  in our nationality but in
our opinions. I think you have already seen this in this debate today, but I think I can
assure you that, despite some fundamenta l philosophical differences, I believe all
Pacific MPs work for the better of our community. We have Alfred Ngaro and Sam
Lotu-Iiga, leaders in their communities, on the other side of the House. I do honestly
believe their plans are to li ft their communities in their regions and the Pacific. The
problem is, we just disagree how we go about it. That is the beau ty of the democracy
that we live in, and that we as Pasifika are pa rticipating in it is a sign that Pasifika are
well and truly a force—a growing force—in politics here in New Zealand.
Can I also acknowledge the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, led by
John Hayes, for organising this forum and th is event over the w eekend. I know it has
been an interesting task. The programme fo r the weekend and the 3 or 4 days ahead
looks great, and I look forward to hosting you all in Porirua on Sunday evening.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: We—we.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: We look forward to it—pan-political. To the 70 members of the
delegation from the 22 Pacifi c nations, taloha ni and t ēnā koutou katoa. I look forward
to the next 4 days as we in New Zealand di scuss and, as Sam Lotu-I iga said, hear from
you about the issues that are im portant to the Pacific. I w ould in particular like to
acknowledge Margaret Pedro and Tavita Pu e from Tokelau, malo ni. As a proud
Tokelauan, it is great to have two young l eaders from Nukunonu and Fakaofo here to
ensure there is a strong Pacific voice from Tokelau. For those who are at home watching
or listening, Tokelau is a proud small nation of three atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu, and
Fakaofo.
It is an interesting time to be a Pacific MP. As I said, we are now well entrenched on
the political stage, but as we move towards a Pasifika community that is becoming more
New Zealand - born, new opportunities and ch allenges emerge. Attitudes are changing,
but it is important that our values do not. Many of you may have seen that last night in a
debate in our Parliament on the issue of marriage equality. I felt compelled to ensure the
diversity of views in the Pacific community were represented, but in doing that I needed
to respect the view of others, although I disagreed. That is one of the challenges. I know
we can overcome it. That is, ensuring that our youth can live in the two worlds they live
in—and some live in three or more—in its simplest form: living in New Zealand, with
Kiwi expectations, and living in our Pacific community, wi th Pacific expectations. It is
not easy, but I look around our communities and this House and I know it can happen.
But enough about us. Let us look at you. In David Shearer’s speech he pointed out
the importance of democracy. He said that  democracy needs a fr ee media. Before I
entered this House my backgr ound was with the media, and I agree with David Shearer
100 percent. We may not like it all the time in New Zealand, but our media have
freedoms, are fearless, and, most of the time, focus on issues that matter to New
Zealanders.
I know that in some places in the Pacifi c the freedom of the media is not so
entrenched. The media in its purest form is  the conduit of the people to hold people like
us to account. I believe we in New Zealand can  do much more to ensure there are free
and skilled media in the Pacific. Tales of to rture of the media, muzzling of the media,
and limited control of the media do nothing to  advance democracy. I am not saying that
we know better; I am saying that we can help to ensure that the right questions are asked
in the pursuit of fair, honest, and accountable representation that is of the people, by the
people, and for the people. I look forward to discussing that tomorrow afternoon.
I would like to pay tribute to our pioneers,  those grandparents and parents, many of
whom came to New Zealand, to a new land, many of them at a young age, to get, as
Sam Lotu-Iiga said, a better life for their families. Someone told me very early on in my
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9577
political career to drop the grateful migrant story, but never, never, never will I do that. I
thank them for making the journey to this land and giving us the opportunity to live
better lives.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: E ngā rangatira katoa o Pasifika, ka nui te mihi ki a
koutou, nō reira, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou katoa. It is a pleasure for me to
take a call in what is a historic debate in this Chamber in the presence of our Pacific
politicians, participants, and political leaders. It is especially significant for me, as a
Pacific-born Indian, as a F ijian person who lived there, grew up there, received the
wisdom of the people of Fiji, and being from a family with a long history and tradition
in Fiji. That is what I brought to New Zealand years ago and it is what sustains me here.
Those of us who are from the Pacific can ne ver be from anywhere else. So for that
reason it is a special pleasure.
I want to acknowledge all of you who are here, welcome you warmly, and add my
weight to others who have already welcom ed you. In particular, however, I want to
acknowledge the five participants from Fiji.  These are young people and they represent
the future of Fiji. They will be the new lead ers, and I know your task is more difficult
than those whom you sit alongside at the moment, but know that you, in this Parliament
and in the time you are here, are warmly welcome and will be as warmly supported as
you need to be. I know that you will pick up much to take back to our homeland and
contribute to what needs to be done there.
I also acknowledge all those who have work ed hard to make this particular forum
possible—those who started in 2006, and those, like John Hayes and the present Foreign
Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, who ha ve made this possible, together with the
officials who have made it possible as well.
What I value most as a member of Parliame nt and as a New Zealander is the ability
of citizens to decide who is going to govern th em, and then to change them if they are
not performing. Sometimes that is called demo cracy. But it is the ability of people who
are ruled to decide who is going to be their Government. I have heard it said sometimes
that democracies are a Western concept, desi gned for a different environment, and not
relevant everywhere. I do refute that. The system of people deciding who will rule them
and when to throw them out belongs to th e people. There is much more that goes
alongside a democracy. When a democratic sy stem does not work, we try to find out
what the reasons are for it not working, and change them. We do not change the system.
There is no other system that I know of that produces the kinds of results that
democracies produce that enable people to acces s their rights, etc. So for that reason I
support democracies and I support a system where people rule.
Some democracies are confused with the workings of Government. The workings of
Government are not necessarily equal to democracies. They are quite different concepts.
If Governments do not work, then change the Government. It does not mean that
democracies have not worked.
Democracy represents many things, but ce rtainly it is the sum total of all the
institutions that have been developed to en able the people to c hoose a Government on
the basis of the policies and manifestos th ey have put forward. It includes a clean
electoral system, a system of voting where a ll votes are equal, a predictable transition
when Governments change, a free media, an independent judiciary, proper separation of
powers, a military that is totally subject to the will of Parliament, effective agencies to
provide public services, and a system for people to access their rights. Those are the
tools, and when these things work together, which is the case in New Zealand, then in
this Chamber we can debate any issue. We can argue with each other, and we can go out
and still be friends, but knowing that the Government is being held accountable. The
Opposition has a role.
9578 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
So the gift of democracy is a huge one, and if  there is a gift that New Zealand has to
offer, it is to demonstrate this democracy. And today, tomorrow, Saturday, Sunday, and
Monday that is what we will be doing—dem onstrating our democracy to you. What I
regret is that the county of my birth is still struggling with this—not through the actions
of the people who elect Governments, nor—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora t ātau katoa ng ā whanaunga i haere mai i tawhiti. E Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, haere
mai, e rarau ki roto i te Whare nei. Ahakoa t ōna āhua, he āhua P ākehā nei i t ōna
mutunga anā, kua noho nei m ātau te iwi M āori ki konei ki te kawe i ng ā wawata o Te
Ao Māori. Tēnā koutou, haere mai, haere mai, haere mai rā.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Salutations to y ou all, the relatives who have come here
from afar. Welcome to you, the great ocean of Kiwa, settle into this House. Even though
this setting is somewhat European-like, we the M āori members have eventually become
part of this scene to bear the aspirations of M āoridom. Acknowledgments to you
collectively, welcome, welcome, and welcome indeed.]
When the M āori Party acknowledged the relations hip between tangata whenua and
the people, our brothers and sisters of the Pacific, Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, and as we
travelled from Hawaiki we shared an anci ent knowledge of the stars and the oceans.
That knowledge is passed down to us, to this  day, in our tukutuku panels that adorn the
walls of our carved whare throughout the motu. Today, in this place, we pay tribute to
the rich oral traditions of our ancient navigators who guided us from the past to this
future. From our whakapapa connections, our  genealogical connections, we have an
obligation to support the well-being of our br others and sisters in the Pacific as M āori.
As our closest neighbours, our security, stability, and prosperity are closely linked. On a
personal level our people interact every day an d must unite to face the challenges that
we all experience.
We say that the strength of Māori and Pasifika peoples lies in our āinga, our whānau,
our communities who pull together to bring change for ourselves. Our key priority,
whānau ora, has been describe d by our Pasifika relations, our Pasifika whanaunga, as
restoring the role of the village. We stand together in the pursuit of mana motuhake. We
support Pasifika nations in growing their own local accountability and success, rather
than foisting a system of private enterprise upon them that may not fit either the culture
or the people. Our view in the M āori Party is that we should assist rather than dominate
development. We support Pasifika nations in  their journey to real ise their own modern
aspirations on their own land, in line with their own tikanga and their own traditions.
Here in Aotearoa we have provided a place to live for ma ny people who call the
Pacific home. Just as in M āori communities where young people leave their papak āinga
for urban areas, those left at home feel the loss of their most talented and those who
have left feel a loss of c onnection. We must support our Pa sifika relations to remain
connected to their homelands, maintaining th e essence of who they are. We call this
rangatiratanga; others might say mana mot uhake—the ability to be strong in your own
identity, language, and culture. We think the key for any peoples lies in developing their
own solutions as a more effective, effici ent, and enduring response. We believe in
greater community development, and less governmental bureaucracy. The focus of the
Māori Party is to bring to fruition the aspirations of New Zealanders through self-
determination, kaupapa tuku iho, and a commitm ent to the Treaty of Waitangi. In the
Pacific we would expect the same—that your own forms of bus iness and governance,
which were in place many years prior to the ar rival of the Palagi European colonisation,
will stand you in good stead for the generations to come.
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9579
It is wonderful to have you all here—our relations—and I want to finish by paying
tribute to all of the Pasifika brot hers and sisters who have stood by M āori in the Land
March of 1975, in the h īkoi of 2004, and in our mutual de sire to honour the Treaty of
Waitangi. Likewise, we have stood by our  Pasifika communities throughout the
traumatic history of the dawn raids in th e 1970s, and in confronting and addressing so
many of the educational, economic, and soci al yardsticks by which our peoples are
measured. Tangata Pasifika and tangata whe nua have always shared a common bond in
our connections through our ancestry, our culture, and our customs. We both understand
implicitly concepts that run to the core of our being. Our land, our whenua, is the central
link to our genealogical connections, as an  enduring umbilical cord, pito, between
yesteryear and tomorrow. I wish all of you de legates who are with us today all the very
best. I look forward to the continuing dialogue that is so vital to our ongoing
relationships with one another.
In closing, I say that I listened earlier and not ed that some of th e parties have been
pitching to you as our vi sitors for your vote. I will not do that myself. Suffice to say,
which of these words sounds sweeter to you, my Pacific br others and sisters? Which
word sounds sweeter, looks sweeter, and ma y be even smells sweeter: New Zealand
First, Labour, National, or Māori? Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: Much of this debate has been about New
Zealand’s relationship with our Pacific ne ighbours, and so it should have been. The
ACT Party acknowledges the importance of these relationships. We celebrate the
contribution that Pasifika communities have made to New Zealand. They have enriched
our society and added to our cultural vibran cy. As Mayor of Auckland for two terms I
had the pleasure of working with, and getting to know and re specting greatly, the
Pacific community of that wonderful multicultural city from where I hail.
In my contribution I want to focus on the obligation we ha ve to our Pacific
neighbours and our Pacific families in our local communities and across this country—
in particular, in the education system. Ever y New Zealand child deserves a world-class
education. There is not much more we can give a young child than unconditional love in
the home and the family, and a world-class education, and I know that Pacific families
are signed up to that proposition.  We have much to do to make this a reality for all our
young people.
So, first, the good news is Pasifika educati on outcomes have improved in all parts of
the education system across th is country. The latest data shows that the number of 2-
year-old to 4-year-old Pasifika enrolmen ts in early childhood education increased by
15.5 percent between 2009 and 2011. The proportion of all Pasifika learners achieving
National Certificate of Edu cational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 qualifications or
equivalent increased from 55 percent in 2009 to 63 percent in 2011. Pasifika learner
take-up of the Youth Guarantee ini tiative was 20 percen t of all young people
participating. Pasifika learners with New Zealand Qualifications Framework level 5
qualification increased from 18 percent to 28 percent in 2011. I would like to
acknowledge the efforts of this National-led Government and, in particular, the Minister
of Education for her efforts in raising ac hievement for Pasifika learners. She is
committed to that cause. I would also like to acknowledge the efforts of our teachers
and the wider Pasifika community for their efforts in helping to raise learner
achievements amongst Pasifika kids.

items.speaker: Now for the bad news
items.text: despite all these improvements, significant challenges remain.
Although New Zealand performs well on the average in the OECD Programme for
International Student Assessment study, we  rate poorly on equity. We are 24 th in the
world, equal with the US. If we were to take  the results for Pasifi ka on their own, we
would be 35th in the world. Although Pasifika participation in early childhood education
9580 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
has increased, it is still the lowest for all population groups. Significant disparities
remain, evidenced in literacy and numeracy  achievements. Disparity in achievement
levels for Pasifika students are significant at the NCEA level and widen further at the
higher qualification level. There is much work  to be done and we need to embrace this
challenge.
There is a wonderful saying that high tides rise all bo ats. We know that when
Pasifika communities are doing well, then the education system in this country is going
to do even better. We know that when Pasifika  kids do well in Auckland, Pasifika kids
are going to do well across the nation, and when they are doing well across the nation,
the high tide will lift the boats across the Pacific countries that you represent.
Can I turn to further good news. Part nership schools are coming, and they can
innovate. We have had very good interest from Pasifika groups  around partnership
schools. They can focus on crea ting a learning environment where every Pasifika child
learns to succeed. They can employ teaching staff who understand and embrace cultural
difference, and cultural difference is critical to  this multicultural society. In short, they
can make a real difference to Pasifika lear ners. I would like to thank the partnership
schools working group and, in particular, Dr Ma rgaret Southwick, a significant Pasifika
educationalist for her great contribution in this policy design. This Government is
absolutely committed to accelerating achievement for Pasifika learners through the
partnership schools initiative and the Pasifika Education Plan 2013-2017. I am
absolutely committed to making sure that every young child, including—

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Can I join with others on behalf
of United Future to welcome our visitors to this Parliament for this important forum. I
have been a member here for nearly 29 years and I am embarrassed to say that this is the
first occasion that I can recall in that time  where such a gathering as this has taken
place. It is long overdue and I hope we do not have to wait another 29 or 30 years for it
to be repeated.
Can I welcome you for the nations that you represent, the diversity of your cultures
and your backgrounds, and say how well that s its alongside the diverse nature of our
society in New Zealand. For my part I am a third-generation Irish New Zealander. My
wife is a direct descendant of New Zeal and’s recognised first European family, a
granddaughter some seven generations down the line. The thing we all have in common,
whatever our background, whatever our cultural roots, whatever our heritage, is that we
live in this part of the world. The issues th at confront this part of the world—be they
related to climate change, be they related to the movement of people, be they related to
economic development—are issues for all of us, and the solutions are ones that we all
have to engage in.
I do not subscribe to the view that New Z ealand is some big sugar daddy on the edge
of the Pacific. I think that is a very patr onising and a very old-fashioned view, and I
think we have to work much more collabo ratively on the things we have in common,
sharing the strengths that we have—and they  will be different from nation to nation—
and the capacities that we have, and they will differ, as well, to assist each one of our
nations to achieve their full potential.
We say that often in respect of our attitude towards young New Zealand children. We
want them all to have the opportunity to reach their full potential in life. So it is with our
relationships with our neighbour s. I do not think that it is  for New Zealand or for any
individual member of the Pacific family to presume a view in respect of other members
of the family. What we need to do is work together to ensure that all of us are capable of
achieving the goals that we want, and they will differ. And in some senses New Zealand
will be the provider of educational opportu nity, of employment, of technology, of
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9581
various other forms of assistance. But in othe r senses it is very much a two-way street,
and we have to recognise the strengths of our Pacific family as we move forward.
One of the things that I think that leads to  in a very immediate sense is the capacity
to assist each other in times of stress. It may be physical stress brought on by adverse
climatic events such as cyclones or storms or whatever, or the mounting threat of
climate change. It may also be unrest brough t on by political or other means. We need
to stand by to help. I think from New Zeal and’s point of view we have to be very
careful that we do not interpret such situat ions as ones where we effectively ration our
assistance—not in financial terms so muc h, but in terms of things like temporary
immigration, in terms of things like family  reunification, where we sometimes take, in
my view, too rigid a position in respect of the nations of the Pacific.
We are all in this part of the world together, and the opportunity that we have may be
on a smaller scale, but it is no different fr om the opportunity that the Europeans have
developed over the last 50 or 60 years. It  is about the capacity to build a unique
community where we work together collabo ratively, respecting the identity and the
integrity of the member nations, but where we speak with a much more unified and
connected voice about the issues that concern us.
I welcome this forum taking place in th is Chamber and elsewhere over the coming
weekend. I think it is a very important develo pment. It is one that is long overdue. I
acknowledge the work of collea gues in this House and else where who have helped to
bring it together. But the real challenge and th e real test of its achievement will be what
flows from this—that is, what procedures, prot ocols, and forms of assistance are put in
place that mean that the goal of  a broad Pacific family, which we often talk about in a
loose-lipped way, can be a goal that is actually achieved in practice. I believe there is
sufficient goodwill on all sides for that to happen, and I look forward to the
deliberations. I encourage the delegates to participate fully. I gi ve you a very warm
welcome to this country. Have a great weekend. It is wonderful to have you here.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Welcome to our Pacific neighbours and dear
friends. I have to say that I am looking forward to going to  the rugby with you
tomorrow night. We will be watching a New Ze aland team dish it out to those Aussies.
But it would be great if, instead of a S uper 15, it was a Super 17 with at least two
Pacific Island teams. I look forward to the time when I can go and visit the islands and
be there to watch a Super 17 rugby game.
Today I will cover three topics, three cha llenges for all Pacific nations: one, have we
preserved and enhanced our heritage; two, have we cared for and protected our
environment, our countries; and, three, ha ve we respected, love d, and cared for our
children? Here in New Zealand we face cha llenges in honouring our obligations to our
children. Some of those challenges incl ude social instability, resulting from a
breakdown of family standards and values, personal unrest, and alienation that comes
from a lack of purpose or ideals. Another challenge we have in New Zealand is some of
the things that we see, a nd I see too much of our land,  technology, and industry being
sold to foreign powers. I see pathways opening for our mineral wealth, onshore and
offshore, to be exploited by overseas intere sts, and throughout the Pacific we share a
common concern in the plundering of fishing stock by foreign fishing powers.
Earlier today a New Zealand First member spoke of political se duction, and it is a
very real threat. New Zealanders only need look back at the news last week, where we
saw our Prime Minister meeting the Chines e Premier with the army out there and
parades and everything. So political seducti on is real, but there is a solution, and I
believe our saving grace is our children. I would implore that the core aim for this
forum is the future well-being of our child ren—to the children of  New Zealand, to the
children of the Pacific. Here in New Zealan d we have more childre n than ever before
9582 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
living in poverty. But what is far worse than poverty is poverty of spirit. The challenge
for all of us here today and this weekend is to raise that spirit, that cultural identity,
within each child of New Zealand and the wi der Pacific. The great challenge, therefore,
is to increase the cultural wealth of each child and each and every family. Therefore, the
goal, or aspiration, must surely be to be aspirational, positive family role models—to
have children say “How do you do that?”, and to live lives where children say “I want to
be able to do that. I want to be like th at.” My mother and my father—positive role
models. And so are my older brother and my older sister.
The pathway for cultural wealth is sure ly education—education of culture and
identity. Who am I? Where do I come from? Where am I going? Spirituality—in New
Zealand we call it wairua. He ritage in spirit, our children’s thoughts and feelings, their
behaviour, awareness of health and of self, and social interaction with families, friends,
and strangers. Personal understanding, knowledge , and awareness. This is cultural
wealth—essential ingredients for every fa mily throughout the Pacific. With major
advances in technology in areas of broadband-enabled devices, such as smartphones and
tablets, the opportunity to educate our families becomes more viable, and also the
opportunity for us as nations to collaborate and communicate more readily, and to share
our knowledge and our technology. For there is a synergy that  binds us, above even our
precious Pacific locations, and that is our  love—our love for our children and our
families. And let that synergy that binds us be honoured by our commitment this
weekend to preserving our resources and e nvironment for our tamariki, our children—
tātou tātou; us and us. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I warmly greet and salute our
visitors from around the Pacific. Thank you very much for coming this way. You show
great stamina here this afternoon. The genesis of today’s debate has come from a variety
of individuals and from the Foreign Affair s, Defence and Trade Committee inquiry into
New Zealand’s relationship w ith the South Pacific. May I acknowledge the drive that
John Hayes, chair of that select committee, has put in to make this event possible. In the
most admirable way he can accurately be accused of borderline belligerence, bullying,
badgering, and bulldozing the select committee members, and a few others. However,
he deserves our heartfelt thanks.
As a fifth-generation New Zealander of Sc ottish, Irish, and English descent, I can
speak only as a relative newcomer to this  region, since about 1831. But like many New
Zealand families, we have intermarried a nd are proudly multicultural. My brother’s
wife, Kuinimeri Aiono Ma’ia’i, from Samoa, has always claimed that the Garden of
Eden was close to Apia, and that the rest of us have a great deal to be thankful for.
Kuinimeri’s brother Dr Semisi Ma’ia’i not only is a fine and distinguished physician but
also wrote the first New Zealand - Samoan  dictionary, an extr aordinary piece of
scholarship and hugely important for our mutual understanding.
Like many other Kiwis, I have  had the chance to explore,  holiday, live, and work in
the wider Pacific. As a young medical student,  I had the adventure of my life in Papua
New Guinea, prior to its independence in  1968, where we set off to go crocodile
hunting, but due to several hiccups in  the planning, I ended up carrying out
immunisation patrols in the central Papuan mountains along the Kokoda Trail—the very
track on which thousands of young Americans and Australians lost their lives to prevent
invasion by the Japanese beyond Port Moresby and on to Australia and New Zealand. If
they had not been successful, the whole Paci fic might be very different today. It has
been indelibly imprinted on me how hard-won our freedom and democracy are and how
potentially fragile they can be. All of us will hope that Fiji can be restored to democracy
as soon as possible, and the in tentions of the superpowers in our region are for stability,
peace, and prosperity.
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9583
I have also had the good fortune to work as  a locum specialist for Dr Toia Alama at
the National Hospital of Samoa in the 1980s. We got to know each other as trainees at
the National Women’s Hospital in New Zealan d, where doctors all over the Pacific do
postgraduate work and then return to thei r homes. The strength of that professional
network is inestimable. I have no doubt that  we in the Pacific should continue to
mutually foster the educationa l and cultural ties that bind us as a region, be they in
medicine, law, business, music, literature, sport, or, of course, politics.
By the way, Wesley College just happens to  be in the Hunua electorate, which I am
privileged to represent. We have ha d some stunning rugby players from that
extraordinary institution. I will never forg et Joeli Vidiri on one wing and Jonah Lomu
on the other, fresh out of school, playing for Counties and smashing the Blues. Thank
you, Fiji. Thank you, Tonga.
The inaugural Pacific forum ahead of us w ill be exciting and worthwhile. It will act
as a conduit to progress our mutual challenge s and aspirations, and remind us that we
are guardians of our environment, that we have led the way in a South Pacific nuclear-
weapon-free zone, and that we must strive for democracy, choice, prosperity, peace, and
true friendship for what my sister-in-law refe rs to as one great Pacific Garden of Eden.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I rise to address the is sue of perhaps greatest
concern of all to humanity. The onset of c limate change, on current emission trends, is
likely to prove dangerous and, according to the World Bank, possibly cataclysmic in the
course of the 21 st century. We have acknowledged the magnitude of future climate
change for about two decades now. What ha s caught us unawares is its imminence.
Climate change is here. Its effects are seen around us as we speak.
Climate change is now seen as a threat to national security and, as the United Nations
Security Council has acknowledged, a potential  threat to intern ational peace and
security—a risk multiplier. Nowhere is this mo re starkly portrayed than in the Pacific.
For our visitors here in this gallery the risk  is existential. The international community
has, to put it simply, failed to solve climate change. It might be argued that an
international community of 193 sovereign States, each pursuing competitive national
advantage, cannot solve a gl obal problem. Not only do we  have a global ecological
crisis but we have a global governance crisis as well. We approach climate like trade
negotiations: punching above our weight, as we heard earlier.  In the presence of our
Pacific neighbours in this House today I apologise for the failure of New Zealand to act
as a responsible global citizen in the matter of climate change.
Among developed countries New Zealand has the worst track record of net emissions
over 20 years—an extraordinary rise of 83 percent from 1990 to 2011. We have tried
but so far have failed. Among developed count ies we stand alone in not having entered
a formal commitment to the UN for reducti ons by 2020. Our informal pledge of 10 to
20 percent conditional is derisory, when the UN had identified 25 to 40 percent and the
Alliance of Small Island States 45 percent. New Zealand sees domestic reductions as an
economic option involving the least cost abatem ent. Pacific countries see it as a moral
imperative involving national survival. Smal l island States have special needs of
relocation. Kiribati has issued a clear appeal to relocate, as may be required, to Australia
and New Zealand. New Zealand has failed to respond adequately.
In 2009 I asked a question of the Prime Minister in this House about his
Government’s plans to receive environmenta l refugees from low-lying Pacific Island

items.speaker: States. The Prime Minister re sponded as follows
items.text: “If one was to look at the Pacific one
would see that the three countries that have  the largest potential exposure to climate
change are Kiribati, Tuvalu, and Tokelau. From New Zealand’s perspective it has a
strong relationship with those countries. Although we will not be setting out exactly
9584 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
what support we would provide those countries if”—if—“a s ituation of climate change
threatened their long-term survival, I think t hose countries could rely on the fact that
New Zealand has a long history with them, would support them, and already has quite a
number of residents from those countries calling New Zealand home.” He continued: “If
that situation occurred—which, it is important to understand, is  likely to be a long way
in the future—it would be my expectation that future New Zealand Governments would
look very sympathetically on that position.” Tr anslation: “I trust that the need does not
come up on my watch, and I am sure Kiwis will prove to be decent if and when the time
comes.”
That was 2009. Today I got pr ecisely the same response from the Prime Minister
virtually word for word. For our national l eader, nothing has changed in 4 years. This
was from a Prime Minister who as recently as  2005 has said that he had his suspicions
about global warming 13 years after all Gove rnments had acknowledged it as a fact in
the 1992 Framework Convention on Climate Change.
I say to the Pacific delegations here today “Welcome to our shores.” Feel free to urge
our country to make it clear today, not in 2050  or even 2020, that we shall receive you
as migrants displaced by climate change, a nd that we stand ready to discuss with you
now—now—plans to that end.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Can I start by saying welcome. Secondly, can I
mention three names that have not been men tioned in this House so far today. One is
Arthur Anae, a former member of Parliament  of Samoan descent, and a member of the
National Party for some time, who served in this House. Taito Phillip Field, who
unfortunately went off the rails, was another member of Samoan descent, and, in fact,
made a pretty big contribution while he was here. In fact, he came in with me 20 years
ago this year. The other one is my brother- in-law Tukoroirangi Morgan. Half of him is
from the Cook Islands. We thi nk of him as being only the M āori MP, the Western
Māori MP, the Te Tai Hau āuru MP, and the king’s spokesp erson, but his other half, his
father, was from the Cooks.
I was born and bred in Ōtara, in “O-town 274”. Let me tell you the names of some of
the families whom I grew up with. I am very proud to have been able to go into each of
their homes and be looked after by the moth ers and fathers of my friends. The Kaleta
family—rest in peace, my brother, Kaleta Kaleta, who died some years ago. There were
the Jackson wh ānau, the Iosefa wh ānau, and the Tafa family—the Tafa family whose
father played a game of cricket with us in Ōtara. He was a stand-in, he was a ring-in, he
smashed Howick, Pakuranga all over the field, and I still remember the cries of despair
from the other team. There were the Tuai family, the Papali’i family, the Tofilau family,
and the Collins family. They were all people I grew up with, and I consider myself to be
a true Pacific Islander. This is a Pacific Is land nation; we just ha ve not thought about it
yet. So I am hopeful that one day in my lifetime we will all cal l ourselves Pacific
Islanders, just not in the way that we think of our brothers and si sters in the Pacific
Islands.
Māori made the long journey to these shores  over 1,000 years ago. Why they left is
beyond me. Who would want to leave an idyl lic neighbourhood such as the Pacific to
come down here to the South Pacific? Maybe it was overcrowding, maybe it was for the
adventure of a lifetime, or maybe it was the re al Kiwi attitude of wanting to know what
was on the other side of the fence. Auckla nd has the biggest concentration of Pacific
Island people in the world. You know, that is on e of the things that we should keep in
the back of our minds every day. It is time Ne w Zealand realised that its true place in
the Pacific is, as I said, as a Pacific Island nation. We need to assi st our brothers and
sisters in the Pacific to be part of the international organisations such as the Inter-
Parliamentary Union and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9585
I have come to despair over the last couple of years that our P acific Island brothers
and sisters cannot even afford to be members of these international organisations. I want
to float some ideas in the last minute or so. Maybe the Pacific Island people can
piggyback on some of our free-trade agr eements. Maybe it is time for a Pacific
Parliament, à la the Rt Hon Mike Moor e’s suggestion 20-odd years ago. We have
common borders. We have citizenship. We have  issues like citizenship. There are three
issues that I get in my office every w eek: immigration, residency, and citizenship,
mainly from the Pacific Islands. It is about  time we started treati ng the Pacific Islands
like our back lawn, with our wh ānau in it, and offer them more than just a few
immigration schemes.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: Kia ora koutou katoa, t ēnei te mihi nui ki a
koutou. It is a very great pleas ure to stand and speak in Pa rliament on this historic
occasion. This is a unique event, and I hope it will not be the last one of its kind.
I was a member of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee at the time
that we did our report into the relations hip between New Zealand and our Pacific
neighbours, and I want to recognise John Hayes and his work as chair of that
committee. Yes, there might have been all of  that bulldozing and bullying and stuff that
went on, but the result was good and it was very well worth it. So I do acknowledge him
and other members of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee at that time.
We are now beginning to reap the benefits of  that report, and this is one of those
moments that have come out of the report.
I recently had the great good fortune and the great honour of visiting the Solomon
Islands. My colleague Dr Cam Calder and I visited the Solomon Islands to talk with
members of Parliament there about the implementation of a report—again, another
