report—that came out of an open forum held  last year on Pacific adolescent sexual
reproduction and health rights. That report ha d a number of recommendations in it, and
one of them was that members of the New Zealand Parliamentarians’ Group on
Population and Development, which is a cr oss-party group, go and talk with members
of Parliament around the Pacific, because th is was a Pacific report. People had come
from Tuvalu, from Papua New Guinea, from  Kiribati, and from around the Pacific to
contribute to that open forum. We heard from  members of Parliament but we also heard
at that time from NGOs—those non-governmental organisations that work in the area of
sexual and reproductive health and rights, particularly with young people.
So I was able at that time to not only advance the agenda that came out of that
combined report with Dr Cam Calder from  the National Party but also I had the
privilege of visiting a part ju st out of Honiara that is called the New Zealand Camp and
saw the places where my father served as a member of the New Zealand Air Force in
World War II. My father never talked about that experience very much. He was one of
that generation who did not discuss what happened in the war much, but I remember
very well having Solomon Islands visitors co me to our house, not in a steady stream,
but visitors who arrived at our house in New Plymouth for years and years and years
afterwards, because my father had known th eir fathers. My father had known their
parents and their families through his posting to the Solomon Islands at that time. It was
a very moving moment for me, and I want to  acknowledge the contribution that, jointly,
the Solomon Islands and New Zealand forces played at that time.
My particular brief is around overseas de velopment assistance, and I have that
responsibility in shadow terms as associate foreign affairs spokesperson. I have always
been concerned about our ability to assist our Pacific neighbours to achieve the United
Nations Millennium Development Goals. We have not engaged sufficiently, I think, in
the achievement of those goals. I hope in the course  of these few days that we will be
able to discuss such things as overseas de velopment assistance so  that we understand
9586 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
exactly what the needs are, so that this is not  seen as the distribution of largesse from a
country that is better off but as an engagement  in partnership to ensure that the peoples
of the Pacific are educated, are healthy, and are well-equipped to make their own
decisions for their own futures. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Very, very warm Pacific greetings to my fellow Pacific
parliamentarians, whom I cannot really see,  but I am assuming you are up there in the
gallery, and I am feeling your beautiful faces.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: I’ll wave for you.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Thank you—thanks, Sam. I am really pleased to take this call for the
Green Party as our women’s spokesperso n and as our Pasi fika, our overseas
development aid, and our human rights spokesp erson. For me, all of those things go
quite nicely together. It is wonderful to be able to talk to you today on some of those
themes. This is my first time of experienci ng—I grew up in a li ttle town down south
that most people think of as quite Palagi, a place called Invercargill. But actually, at the
time I grew up it had the second-highest Po lynesian population, af ter Auckland, in the
world. So you have been part of my growing up . It is really wonderful to have you here
in the House today to give us that sense of th e Pacific here in this House. It is all too
rare an occasion. I hear that some of you were a little shocked by our question time. I
also share that shock every day, so I understa nd. I would also like to offer my thanks to
the Minister for Pacific Island Affairs a nd the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee for hosting this event and promoting this dialogue between us today.
There is so much I could say, because, of course, our relationshi p is long and deep
and there are many things to talk about. Bu t I would like to star t by acknowledging that
New Zealand’s past relationship in the Pacific has been a dual one. It has been at once
an imperialistic and exploitative role, and at the same time many iwi and the K īngitanga
movement have had really strong relationshi ps with many Pacific people. So we have
had these two relationships of solidarity a nd imperialism happening at the same time. I
think we are still sometimes fighting between  those two tensions in our relationships.
As an example, New Zealand is still earni ng more now from the exporting of products
that contribute really strongl y to non-communicable diseases  in your countries than we
are putting into the health budget through official development assistance. I think that in
this discussion we need to be acknowledging some of those tensions.
As the women’s spokesperson, though, I real ly do want to focus on some of the
issues that we share, all of us in the Paci fic. One of those really important issues is
violence against women. Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands have the highest
levels—reported levels at least—in the worl d. We see that in Australia 20 percent of
women experience sexual abuse. In Fiji 66 pe rcent of women are physically abused by
their partners, in Kiribati 68 percent, in the Marshall Islands 30 percent, and in New
Zealand, depending on your figures, between 15 and 30 percent. In Palau and Papua
New Guinea 70 percent of women have experienced gender-based violence, in Samoa it
is 48 percent of women, and in the Solom ons it is 64 percent. In Tonga 23 women a
month are victims of physical assault, in Tuvalu it is one-thir d of women, and in
Vanuatu there have been 3,600 cases reported between 1993 and 2000. Sadly, we do not
even have the data for the Cook Islands, Niue , or the Federated St ates of Micronesia.
This is a shared problem. We are all struggling with this. If we put some focus on it, it is
something we could make a real difference abou t. It would pay off fo r all of us in terms
of our well-being, our health, and our economic benefits.
I am a member, along with some of my  colleagues here, of the New Zealand
Parliamentarians’ Group on Population and Development. We have recognised that
economic development is intrinsically a nd reciprocally linked with sexual and
reproductive health, including maternal health. We have asked our Government to make
18 Apr 2013 Debate On Pacific Issues 9587
a commitment to ring-fencing 15 percent of our overseas development assistance
specifically for sexual and reproductive health. Part of that is a link to the connection to
the violence against women, because if we cannot control our bodies, we cannot control
our destiny. That is around violence, and it is about sexual and reproductive health.
There is a huge difference that all of us coul d make on this issue. I am really looking
forward to having a good dialogue with all of you this weekend on those issues. Kia ora
koutou.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Warm greetings to our
Pacific colleagues. Welcome to the first ever Pacific Parliamentary and Political
Leaders Forum. Welcome to New Zealand.
My background is that I am an elected memb er for an electorate called Rangitata on
the east coast of the South Island. I think it would be fair to say th at there is no other
part of New Zealand that has so few P acific people amongst its population, but the
number is growing. The economy of my el ectorate benefits from the Recognised
Seasonal Employer scheme, and I thank the Pa cific Islands for sending people to work
in my electorate. I hope that the work they are doing in New Zealand is indeed
enriching their lives and assisting their familie s, as it is our economy and our lives. In
fact, I want to say to you that as the num ber of Pacific peoples in my electorate
increases, so too is my community enriched.
As Minister of Women’s Affairs, I am delighted that I can welcome to this forum
over these days the 16 female political lead ers who come from Pacific Island nations. I
want to acknowledge the fact that prior to  me speaking there were two other female
politicians from New Zealand—one from Labour; one from the Greens. I know that our
Minister for Pacific Island Affairs is going to wind up our debate here this afternoon—
again, one of our female politicians. So alt hough we are some, I think, 31 or 32 percent
of this Parliament, we are finishing in style with the women’s voice of this Parliament. I
know that increasing women’s participation in the Pacific legislatures is a challenge. I
acknowledge that challenge. I wish you well in  the different way that each nation is
addressing that challenge. I also wish you success.
I would like to congratulate the Pacific on bringing gender to the forefront. For
example, the 2012 Pacific Leaders Gender Equa lity Declaration renewed the Pacific’s
commitment to improving the lives of wome n and girls. The Pacific Regional Action
Plan on Women, Peace and Security 2012-15 was th e first of its kind in the Pacific. It
enhances women’s security in conflict situations and women’s leadership in conflict
prevention and peace building. In March this year I was absolutely delighted to see the
Pacific play such an active role in th e Commission on the Status  of Women in New
York. It was noted that the Pacific Islands we re playing an increased role, a very much
increased role. I was delighted to be there in amongst it. I would also like to commend
Samoa for leading the Commonwealth Gende r Plan of Action Monitoring Group. The
gender plan of action is the framework through which the Commonwealth contributes to
the advancement of gender equality.
The Pacific’s performance on gender equality  in education also deserves specific
mention. Literacy rates are very high, and significant gains have been made in girls
accessing primary and secondary education in most areas of the Pacific. Congratulations
on your progress in this respect.
New Zealand is a supportive partner for gender equality in the Pacific. In health and
education we work very closely with our de velopment partners to improve access to
education for girls and to strengthen servi ces in maternal and family reproductive
health, and through our aid programme we of fer scholarships to assist women into
tertiary education. Improved infrastructure—p rimarily transport, energy, water, and
9588 Debate On Pacific Issues 18 Apr 2013
telecommunications—also contributes to  economic development and women’s
economic empowerment.
We recently extended the Pacific Preventi on of Domestic Violence Programme to
2016. This is a successful part nership between NZAID, th e New Zealand Police, and
the Pacific Islands chiefs of police. It aims to reduce violence against women and
provide better access to justice for women victims and survivors.
Along with Australia and the US, New Zeal and is supporting the Emerging Pacific
Women’s Leadership Program me. Women leaders from th e 12 Pacific countries are
implementing projects that promote young women leaders and advance women’s
economic opportunities. Women’s economic  empowerment may be enhanced by
improving women’s rights to land ownership,  secure employment, and fair and equal
pay.
As my colleagues before me have ac knowledged, eliminating violence against
women is a struggle we face nationwide. We jo in with you in attempting to address that
struggle here in New Zealand as well.
I close by once again saluting the 16 wome n leaders—political leaders—who have
come to this forum. In fact, I salute all of  the political leaders who have come to this
forum, for improving the lives of women and girls can be done only with our menfolk
helping us. Please enjoy your time in New Zealand. It is wonderful having you here.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana
Whakahaere, otirā, tēnā tātou huri noa i t ō tātou Whare. Kei ngā rangatira o ngā motu o
Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou katoa. T ēnā koutou ng ā
waka katoa e tau mai nei ki Aotearoa ahakoa n ō tēhea o ng ā motu o Te Moana-nui-a-
Kiwa.
[Salutations to you, Mr Speaker, and i ndeed to us throughout our House. Good
afternoon to you, the leaders of the islands of the great sea of Kiwa, acknowledgments
and greetings to you all. I salute you all,  the canoes that have arrived here in New
Zealand, regardless which of the islands in the Pacific you have come from.]
Good afternoon once more, and thank you very much. Can I acknowledge, as
previous speakers have done, your stamina and resilience for the 4 hours that you have
sat there this afternoon watching the debate that has gone on in the House, itching to be
participants in the debate yourselves, which we look forward to occurring from
tomorrow on. Many speakers before me have already commented on how important it is
that this occasion is occurring, how long it ha s actually taken for it occur, and how we
must look forward to continuing this process in the years ahead of us.
Every speaker in this Hous e, no matter which party they have come from, has
participated in the celebration of democracy; of the diversity of our country Aotearoa
New Zealand; and of the direct  links between members of Parliament on all sides of the
House who are of Pacific descent, all of us w ho are of Polynesian descent, and all of us
who are descendants of navigato rs and adventurers, who set out from other parts of the
world with a clear conviction that there was something better for them and their families
and their descendants, as you too reflect in your  own parts of the Pacific. We are
gathered here in our unity of being sons  and daughters of the Pacific, committed to
creating a better legacy for t hose who will follow us. We jo in, despite our differences,
whatever those may be, in our commitment  to creating a better world. I thank you for
your participation this af ternoon and look forward to it over the next 2 days. T ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.
Motion agreed to.
18 Apr 2013 Sittings of the House 9589

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Given the progress in the Pasifika
debate, I seek leave for the House to rise early, and I wish our Pacific colleagues a
successful weekend.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is
there any objection? There is no objection.
Can I just welcome our guests from overseas. I look forward, over the next 4 days, to
your participation. From tomorrow it will be y our turn to be down here, debating those
issues of interest to you, and we look forward to your pa rticipation during the next 4
days.
The House adjourned at 5.58 p.m.

have more questions than answers for you, but  I am certainly here to listen and learn

powers, a military that is totally subject to the will of Parliament, effective agencies to 
provide public services, and a system for people to access their rights. Those are the 
tools, and when these things work together, which is the case in New Zealand, then in 
this Chamber we can debate any issue. We can argue with each other, and we can go out 
and still be friends, but knowing that the Government is being held accountable. The 
Opposition has a role.

JAN LOGIE (Green) : Very, very warm Pacific greetings to my fellow Pacific 
parliamentarians, whom I cannot really see,  but I am assuming you are up there in the 
gallery, and I am feeling your beautiful faces. 
Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga: I’ll wave for you. 
JAN LOGIE: Thank you—thanks, Sam. I am really pleased to take this call for the 
Green Party as our women’s spokesperso n and as our Pasi fika, our overseas 
development aid, and our human rights spokesp erson. For me, all of those things go 
quite nicely together. It is wonderful to be able to talk to you today on some of those 
themes. This is my first time of experienci ng—I grew up in a li ttle town down south 
that most people think of as quite Palagi, a place called Invercargill. But actually, at the 
time I grew up it had the second-highest Po lynesian population, af ter Auckland, in the 
world. So you have been part of my growing up . It is really wonderful to have you here 
in the House today to give us that sense of th e Pacific here in this House. It is all too 
rare an occasion. I hear that some of you were a little shocked by our question time. I 
also share that shock every day, so I understa nd. I would also like to offer my thanks to 
the Minister for Pacific Island Affairs a nd the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade 
Committee for hosting this event and promoting this dialogue between us today.  
There is so much I could say, because, of course, our relationshi p is long and deep 
and there are many things to talk about. Bu t I would like to star t by acknowledging that 
New Zealand’s past relationship in the Pacific has been a dual one. It has been at once 
an imperialistic and exploitative role, and at the same time many iwi and the K īngitanga 
movement have had really strong relationshi ps with many Pacific people. So we have 
had these two relationships of solidarity a nd imperialism happening at the same time. I 
think we are still sometimes fighting between  those two tensions in our relationships. 
As an example, New Zealand is still earni ng more now from the exporting of products 
that contribute really strongl y to non-communicable diseases  in your countries than we 
are putting into the health budget through official development assistance. I think that in 
this discussion we need to be acknowledging some of those tensions.  
As the women’s spokesperson, though, I real ly do want to focus on some of the 
issues that we share, all of us in the Paci fic. One of those really important issues is 
violence against women. Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands have the highest 
levels—reported levels at least—in the worl d. We see that in Australia 20 percent of 
women experience sexual abuse. In Fiji 66 pe rcent of women are physically abused by 
their partners, in Kiribati 68 percent, in the Marshall Islands 30 percent, and in New 
Zealand, depending on your figures, between 15 and 30 percent. In Palau and Papua 
New Guinea 70 percent of women have experienced gender-based violence, in Samoa it 
is 48 percent of women, and in the Solom ons it is 64 percent. In Tonga 23 women a 
month are victims of physical assault, in Tuvalu it is one-thir d of women, and in 
Vanuatu there have been 3,600 cases reported between 1993 and 2000. Sadly, we do not 
even have the data for the Cook Islands, Niue , or the Federated St ates of Micronesia. 
This is a shared problem. We are all struggling with this. If we put some focus on it, it is 
something we could make a real difference abou t. It would pay off fo r all of us in terms 
of our well-being, our health, and our economic benefits.  
I am a member, along with some of my  colleagues here, of the New Zealand 
Parliamentarians’ Group on Population and Development. We have recognised that 
economic development is intrinsically a nd reciprocally linked with sexual and 
reproductive health, including maternal health. We have asked our Government to make

specifically for sexual and reproductive health. Part of that is a link to the connection to 
the violence against women, because if we cannot control our bodies, we cannot control

There is a huge difference that all of us coul d make on this issue. I am really looking 
forward to having a good dialogue with all of you this weekend on those issues. Kia ora 
koutou. 
Hon JO GOODHEW (Minister of Women’s Affairs) : Warm greetings to our 
Pacific colleagues. Welcome to the first ever Pacific Parliamentary and Political 
Leaders Forum. Welcome to New Zealand. 
My background is that I am an elected memb er for an electorate called Rangitata on 
the east coast of the South Island. I think it would be fair to say th at there is no other 
part of New Zealand that has so few P acific people amongst its population, but the 
number is growing. The economy of my el ectorate benefits from the Recognised 
Seasonal Employer scheme, and I thank the Pa cific Islands for sending people to work 
in my electorate. I hope that the work they are doing in New Zealand is indeed 
enriching their lives and assisting their familie s, as it is our economy and our lives. In 
fact, I want to say to you that as the num ber of Pacific peoples in my electorate 
increases, so too is my community enriched. 
As Minister of Women’s Affairs, I am delighted that I can welcome to this forum 
over these days the 16 female political lead ers who come from Pacific Island nations. I 
want to acknowledge the fact that prior to  me speaking there were two other female 
politicians from New Zealand—one from Labour; one from the Greens. I know that our 
Minister for Pacific Island Affairs is going to wind up our debate here this afternoon—
again, one of our female politicians. So alt hough we are some, I think, 31 or 32 percent 
of this Parliament, we are finishing in style with the women’s voice of this Parliament. I 
know that increasing women’s participation in the Pacific legislatures is a challenge. I 
acknowledge that challenge. I wish you well in  the different way that each nation is 
addressing that challenge. I also wish you success. 
I would like to congratulate the Pacific on bringing gender to the forefront. For 
example, the 2012 Pacific Leaders Gender Equa lity Declaration renewed the Pacific’s 
commitment to improving the lives of wome n and girls. The Pacific Regional Action 
Plan on Women, Peace and Security 2012-15 was th e first of its kind in the Pacific. It 
enhances women’s security in conflict situations and women’s leadership in conflict 
prevention and peace building. In March this year I was absolutely delighted to see the 
Pacific play such an active role in th e Commission on the Status  of Women in New 
York. It was noted that the Pacific Islands we re playing an increased role, a very much 
increased role. I was delighted to be there in amongst it. I would also like to commend 
Samoa for leading the Commonwealth Gende r Plan of Action Monitoring Group. The 
gender plan of action is the framework through which the Commonwealth contributes to 
the advancement of gender equality. 
The Pacific’s performance on gender equality  in education also deserves specific 
mention. Literacy rates are very high, and significant gains have been made in girls 
accessing primary and secondary education in most areas of the Pacific. Congratulations 
on your progress in this respect. 
New Zealand is a supportive partner for gender equality in the Pacific. In health and 
education we work very closely with our de velopment partners to improve access to 
education for girls and to strengthen servi ces in maternal and family reproductive 
health, and through our aid programme we of fer scholarships to assist women into 
tertiary education. Improved infrastructure—p rimarily transport, energy, water, and

telecommunications—also contributes to  economic development and women’s 
economic empowerment. 
We recently extended the Pacific Preventi on of Domestic Violence Programme to 
2016. This is a successful part nership between NZAID, th e New Zealand Police, and 
the Pacific Islands chiefs of police. It aims to reduce violence against women and 
provide better access to justice for women victims and survivors. 
Along with Australia and the US, New Zeal and is supporting the Emerging Pacific 
Women’s Leadership Program me. Women leaders from th e 12 Pacific countries are 
implementing projects that promote young women leaders and advance women’s 
economic opportunities. Women’s economic  empowerment may be enhanced by 
improving women’s rights to land ownership,  secure employment, and fair and equal 
pay. 
As my colleagues before me have ac knowledged, eliminating violence against 
women is a struggle we face nationwide. We jo in with you in attempting to address that 
struggle here in New Zealand as well. 
I close by once again saluting the 16 wome n leaders—political leaders—who have 
come to this forum. In fact, I salute all of  the political leaders who have come to this 
forum, for improving the lives of women and girls can be done only with our menfolk
